#8776. U.S. Women Could Be Upgraded to World Half Marathon Gold After Kenyan Runner’s EPO Ban

Jess McClain, Weini Kelati, and Emma Grace Hurley could earn gold as a team after Veronica Loleo's doping suspension.

Emma Grace Hurley, Weini Kelati, and Jess McClain already had plenty to celebrate after earning the United States its first women's team medal at September's World Road Running Championships in Copenhagen. But nearly two months after finishing with silver, the American trio could soon have gold added to their résumés.

On Thursday, November 19, the Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) announced that Kenya's Veronica Loleo had received a three-year doping ban after testing positive for erythropoietin (EPO), a prohibited substance. The decision officially disqualifies her second-place finish at the September 20 event, where her silver medal helped Kenya secure the women's team title. But with Loleo's result now thrown out, Kenya's team score has to be recalculated. Countries are ranked by the combined finishing times of their three fastest athletes, and Loleo’s removal means Kenya must now count Lilian Kasait Rengeruk, who finished 34th in 1:10:36, potentially lifting the U.S. to first place in the team standings.

The Kenyan women originally led with a combined 3:17:33, ahead of the Americans' 3:19:51. But removing Loleo's 1:06:05 pushes Kenya's total to 3:22:04, leaving the U.S. in first place by two minutes and 13 seconds. Kenya would drop to second and Ethiopia would remain third, although World Athletics has yet to officially confirm the updated results.

Hurley recently acknowledged the uncertainty in a comment on Citius Mag's Instagram, noting that nobody can know exactly how the race would've unfolded without Loleo. Still, she admitted, "it would've been so cool to celebrate gold 🥹."

Loleo's sample was collected during an out-of-competition test on September 6 ahead of the championships, two weeks prior to the competition. She initially told investigators she couldn't explain the positive result, mentioning an injection she'd received for an injury, but later admitted to the violation on October 30, which earned her a one-year reduction from the standard four-year suspension.

Loleo wasn't the only major Kenyan distance runner to receive a final decision Thursday. Peres Jepchirchir, the reigning world marathon champion and 2021 Olympic gold medalist, was also handed a three-year ban following an EPO finding.

“The Kenyan authorities have made a lot of progress in the fight against doping in the last five years, but these cases highlight that there is still a long way to go,” AIU chief executive Brett Clothier said in a statement.

“The Kenyan government is aware of the current situation and has committed to further strengthen the Anti-Doping Agency of Kenya and take action to address the criminal networks that facilitate doping within the country.”

Jepchirchir, who had been provisionally suspended in October, has accepted the disqualification of her results dating back to July 17, including her August victory at the Sydney Marathon. Fellow Kenyan Irine Cheptai is expected to inherit that title.

#8774. This Mileage Target Can Help You Determine Whether You Built a Strong Enough Base to Start Race Training

Use it to bridge the gap between your current routine and your next training plan.

Base training involves spending a few weeks running at an easy pace and slowly increasing your mileage over time. It’s a crucial first step in any running journey, designed to help you ease into race-specific training.

Building a sufficient aerobic base helps you avoid the aches and pains that come with ramping up mileage too quickly, especially if you’ve been running sporadically or took some time off. It also makes running feel more doable, as it bridges the gap between your current routine and your goal training plan.

The hard part of this foundational phase? Figuring out if you’re ready to tackle the first few weeks of a plan and start race-specific workouts. Thankfully, coaches offer a helpful benchmark to hit, plus they explain how to smoothly transition your base routine to race training, without shocking your system.

Building a strong base before racing any distance helps prevent injuries and improves long-term performance, including improved aerobic capacity, endurance, faster recovery, mental conditioning, and weight and stress management, Jill Becker, a personal trainer and run coach at Life Time in Westminster, CO, previously told Runner’s World. That’s why the phase is necessary for all runners, whether you’re new to the sport or have a Boston qualifying time on the list of goals.

“Even a 5K race relies heavily on aerobic systems for energy production—so the better the aerobic base you have, the faster you can race,” Laura Norris, owner and coach at Laura Norris Running in Boulder, CO, previously told Runner’s World.

Additionally, Norris says doing these easy miles weeks before your goal training block allows your body to adapt to the mileage first, so you can then add in speedwork leading up to race day with lower risk of injury and burnout. Taking this approach helps you avoid increasing volume and intensity at the same time, which can often lead to overtraining.

Finally, tackling a base phase means you’ll feel more confident heading into, say, a four-miler with faster-paced efforts (like tempo or race pace miles), as you’ll have already run four miles at an easy pace consistently for several weeks.

Building a strong base requires covering a certain number of miles consistently over the course of several weeks. Beginners should aim to spend at least 10 weeks on this training block, while intermediate runners can follow a six-week plan, and more advanced runners typically need about four weeks to set that aerobic foundation, Becker says.

If you’ve already picked out your training plan, Norris recommends working up to at least 80 percent of the weekly mileage prescribed in the first week of that plan. For example, our 20-week beginner marathon plan prescribes 12 miles in the first week. That means you’ll want to work up to about 10 miles per week before diving into the plan. If you’re looking to break two hours in the half marathon, which requires running at least 18 miles in the first week of the Runner’s World plan, then you’ll want to work up to about 15 miles.

If you haven’t identified your training plan yet, Becker recommends adding at least 10 miles to your current weekly volume. (If you’re currently running 10 miles a week, work up to 20.)

Look for a plan that builds up to that mileage goal slowly, following the 10 percent rule, which means increasing your mileage by no more than 10 percent each week.

Keep in mind, base training is about setting the foundation for your next training block, and a part of that process should include recovery time. This means making time for rest days and down weeks (in which you reduce your volume to allow for recovery and better performance), as well as staying on top of your nutrition, sleep habits, and cross-training.

Monique LeBrun is a health and fitness editor who is based in Easton, Pennsylvania. She covers a wide range of health and wellness topics, with a primary focus on running performance and nutrition. #8773. 5 Yoga Poses to Get You Through Any Holiday Gathering

Certain seasons come with a lot, and we mean a lot, of socializing. On the one hand, this means a chance to spend quality time with family and friends, which is always a win. But if you deal with any amount of social anxiety, gatherings can also come with stress and general overwhelm.

If leaving isn’t an option—just kidding, we know you probably want to be there—there are ways to find grounding and calm within your own being. You can practice breathwork, take a walk, even excuse yourself and enjoy a yoga pose or two for a minute. Or, if you resonate with the asanas on this list, perhaps five!

These yoga poses are meant to be easily accessible. Escape for a few moments to try one of the more involved poses or enjoy a super subtle modification mid-party!

Holiday gatherings tend to involve a fair amount of standing around—which is where your casual Tree Pose (Vrksasana) comes in. Popping one foot up—whether against your upper or lower leg or, more stealthily, your ankle—can be done at literally any time: while you’re doing the dishes, chatting with loved ones, or experiencing a lull in activity. The reminder that you’re in control of your sense of balance can help you feel steadier on your own two feet in all ways.

Folding forward can provide a sense of tremendous release and relief. Hinging at your hips in Standing Forward Bend (Uttanasana) and allowing your head and upper body to hang heavy—sometimes referred to as Rag Doll—serves as a subtle inversion, activating your parasympathetic nervous system and encouraging calm. Plus, this pose is normal enough to fold into at any point. Just tell your people that you need a quick stretch.

Finding strength within yourself can make chilling out a little easier. Pressing up—or jumping back—into Plank Pose activates your core, arms, and legs, then asks you to pause. Turning your focus toward this physical task, whether for a few breaths or a full minute, can help snap you out of an anxious spin and get you back into a celebratory state.

Sometimes, the best thing you can do is retreat to a spare bedroom (or the couch or the floor) and lie down for a while. Savasana can certainly provide some calming release, but for something a little more likely to get you out of your head and into your body, try Reclining Bound Angle Pose. It’s a subtle stretch that rejuvenates without being daunting—sort of like a best-case-scenario social engagement.

#8772. The 7 Best Garmin Watches for Cyclists: Editor-Tested Picks for Training, Recovery, and Everyday Wear

Skip the bike computer? These Garmin watches can track rides, workouts, sleep, and recovery.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Cyclists, myself included, are often data driven. Even for cyclists that aren’t particularly motivated to optimize their performance there’s a belief that if a ride, run, hike, or any activity isn’t on Strava, it didn’t happen. Tracking your rides is easy to do with a head unit, but the tracking is limited to just the time spent on your bike.

Many riders and multisport athletes just don’t need a dedicated bike computer—especially with how smart smartwatches have become over the last few years. Smartwatches offer many of the same features that you find on bike computers, but smartwatches can also track sleep, heart rate, and activities you do off the bike. I have a few friends who even track mowing their lawn to make sure they don’t lose out on the activity for the day. With so many smartwatches out there, it can be hard to pick which one to choose, but time and again we go back to Garmin as the benchmark for tracking tech.

Tracking three back-to-back activities can be an annoyance for data-hungry triathletes. However, the Forerunner 970’s “Triathlon” mode gives multisport athletes the freedom to change between workouts without ending their activity. You only need to tap the lap button at the start and end of each transition. However, the 970 is a great option for folks who aren’t also swimming and running on their bike rides.

While I’m not a triathlete, I’ve been testing the 970 for a couple of weeks during road rides, commutes, and my daily routine; my overall impression is quite positive. This is a performance-optimized smartwatch for performance-minded athletes. It can track and measure seemingly every data point across an enormous range of sports and activities. Specifically related to cycling, the Forerunner 970 has preset profiles for: Road, mountain biking, gravel, commuting, touring, e-biking, eMTB riding, indoor, cyclocross, and BMX. If none of those options meet your niche, you can also create your own.

The variety and specificity of data you can track with the Forerunner 970 is mind-boggling. If you want to measure or see something related to riding, you probably can—although finding it in the array of options is sometimes the hardest part. And like Garmin’s head units, that’s the watch’s biggest downside. Garmin packs so many options into its devices that it can be difficult to navigate within the screens. Luckily, the Garmin Connect app is (mostly) easy to use, and changes made in the app instantly push to the phone.

A feature I like on the 970 is the ability to “Lap by Location”. With this turned on, your watch will automatically start a new lap each time you pass through that GPS location again. That means no more forgetting to tap “Lap” when you’re deep in the red zone with one lap to go in an event. This makes the 970 perfect for cyclocross, criterium, and XC mountain bike racers seeking to track in-race performance data at a granular level.

The Venu 4’s sleek, not-too-techy profile allows you to maximize your smartwatch mileage, both during workouts and in daily life. It prioritizes general smartwatch functionality, but there’s still plenty of processing power. That makes the Venu great for all-day wear, both on and off the bike.

Senior Art Director, Colin McSherry, has tested the Venu 4 against his trusty Forerunner. He notes the Venu‘s solid 12-day battery life is closer to 8 to 10 days when heavily using route navigation for cycling, running, and hiking. He also said, “I found the navigation a bit simpler and easier to use compared to the Garmin Forerunner 970 due to fewer physical buttons.”

On the bike, starting and tracking a workout is easy. McSherry noted that, “GPS does take a few seconds to register, but usually picks up as you are taking your first few pedal strokes.” Compared to his Wahoo Elemnt, he found the GPS data was very close. “So if I forgot my computer or wanted to get away from staring at a screen while on a ride, it’s a great way to track basic metrics,” he said.

Garmin released the Fēnix 9 this fall, but we still love the Fēnix 8—and there are some great deals on the watch right now. The 8 Pro is Garmin’s flagship model in its class-leading Fēnix lineup. This watch is packed with virtually every feature you could want to measure and manage your outdoor adventures. The Fēnix 8 Pro includes it all in a rugged design featuring dive-rated buttons, a crisp AMOLED display (or MicroLED for an extra $400), and a titanium bezel. The device connects via ANT+ or Bluetooth to third-party sensors and supports a wide range of activity profiles.

However, the Fēnix 8 Pro’s biggest upgrade is the included inReach satellite/LTE connectivity. (You previously needed a separate Garmin inReach device for that.) For backcountry adventurers, the ability to message, call, share location, or trigger SOS from your wrist is a must-have feature. All that capability comes at a cost—in both price and battery life. Garmin claims up to 15 days of battery life (in smartwatch mode) for the 47mm model and 27 days for the 51mm version. However, those numbers drop when LTE or satellite features are active.

Jason Griffin, Senior Health and Fitness Editor, is currently testing the 8 Pro. He said, “It’s smarter than I expected a watch could be,” and notes that “answering calls through the watch is super easy, and tracking both rides and runs is intuitive.” He added, “The flashlight was great to find things in the middle of the night while I was holding my sleeping toddler.”

While the Forerunner 265 is an older model, we find it strikes a good balance between Garmin’s budget-minded watches and its thousand-dollar devices. The 265’s accuracy is top-tier for its price, and this model has a far more readable display than its predecessor, thanks to a bright OLED screen—a near-critical feature if you don’t want to take your hands off your grips for too long to check your mileage.

If you have smaller wrists (or prefer a more compact watch), the Forerunner 265S is a great choice. It’s lighter, slimmer, and even offers longer battery life.

Garmin’s new Forerunner 70 isn’t really an update of its long-running Forerunner 55 entry-level model: the 70 is an entirely new device. The new model has a larger display, tons more features, and (most importantly for cyclists) many more bicycle profile options.

The Forerunner 70 is designed to be a great running watch, and its features and data logging abilities are best for off-bike activities. However, the 70 is still a good option for fitness-minded riders or cyclists needing to log their rides and basic training data. So, while the 70 cannot connect to your power meter or smart trainer, it still features solid GPS tracking, a heart rate monitor, and it can follow pre-planned courses.

Buying Tip: If you need to track power, spend the extra $50 and upgrade to the Forerunner 170 model.

Garmin released the Enduro 4 this fall and we are currently testing it to see how it compares to the Enduro 3. The Enduro 3 is still a great option from Garmin and is on sale right now. The Enduro 3 is what happens when you take the top-shelf performance of the Fēnix and optimize it for maximum battery life. It’s a high-caliber solar watch that can last a staggering 36 days in smartwatch mode and up to 150 hours in GPS mode. It’s perfect for long bikepacking outings to places lacking spots to recharge.

At 51mm, the watch face is large but surprisingly unobtrusive. It feels light (63 grams) and comfortable on the wrist, even during long rides. The Enduro also has a sleeker profile than many premium smartwatches, with fewer sharp edges and oversized buttons. A feature our tester didn’t know they needed is the built-in flashlight. It works very well and is unexpectedly useful in everyday situations.

While the Velcro strap may not win style points off the bike, it’s incredibly functional. It allows for a perfectly snug fit, unlike traditional watch bands (frequently, one loop is too tight and the next is too loose).

Garmin markets the Forerunner 170 Music as a running watch, but that label doesn’t do it justice. It’s a true multi-sport smartwatch, built to support a wide range of activities—including multiple cycling disciplines—and it connects to ANT+ and Bluetooth sensors for more detailed ride data and notifications.

As the name suggests, it includes 4GB of onboard storage for music. This means you can leave your phone behind and still have your playlist. It also features an altimeter, barometer, compass (ABC sensors), a pulse oximeter, and advanced tracking tools, making it capable in almost any scenario.

If you participate in various outdoor activities, you may prefer to own a single device to track everything. Whether cycling, running, hiking, paddling, walking the dog, or playing pickleball, a Garmin watch offers powerful, versatile functionality in a streamlined profile that’s always with you.

If you regularly track multiple types of workouts, while many road and gravel riders prefer cycling head units for instant access to maps, routing details, power metrics, and other data, some riders prefer smartwatches for logging ride data.

Not needing to learn or own multiple overlapping devices simplifies and declutters your life. And in his excellent story, “The Problem with Modern Cycling Computers Isn’t the Huge Screens,” Test Editor Dan Chabanov argues that many head units are bloated with unnecessary functions.

Mountain bikers who often ride technical trails (bike park riders and enduro racers, for example) are increasingly turning to watches to document rides. With some cycling computers costing upwards of $1,000, you don’t want it dangling off the front of your bar or attached to your top tube in the event of a crash. Additionally, a computer is sometimes an unwanted distraction when trying to concentrate on a challenging descent.

Triathletes and duathlon racers are another group of riders who often prefer smartwatches. Watches allow athletes to transition between segments without needing to change devices or combine files after an event. Similarly, since the discipline involves swapping out muddy bikes in the pits during a race, cyclocross racers often use smartwatches.

A quick spin through Garmin’s website reveals a dizzying lineup of watches—sleek, feature-packed, and often overwhelming to sort through. While nearly all of them include the core functions you’d expect from a sports smartwatch, four series stand out as the best options for cyclists: Forerunner, Enduro, Fēnix, and Venu.

The Forerunner series is Garmin’s core watch for cyclists and multisport athletes. It includes five models, starting with the $250 Forerunner 70, which covers the basics, and going up to the $750 Forerunner 970, which combines high-end smartwatch features with advanced training and navigation tools.

The Enduro is designed for endurance athletes and offers the longest battery life of any Garmin watch. It includes the premium features of a cycling computer and smartwatch, along with extras such as solar charging and a built-in flashlight—making it a great option for long adventures.

The Fēnix series shares many advanced features with the Enduro line—activity profiles, multisport tracking, and smartwatch tools—but adds specialized options for adventurers and divers. Fēnix has a slightly shorter battery life than the Enduro, and the watch faces are smaller.

Finally, the Venu is another option. It blends performance training, GPS, and data tracking features with fashion-forward styling. So, it looks good on and off the bike.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#8771. For Years, Doctors Blamed My Mysterious Symptoms on Running. A Simple Blood Test Proved Them Wrong.

All along, running actually helped me feel better.

This article originally appeared in the Spring 2025 issue of Runner’s World.

Running and menstruation entered my life around the same time, at age 13. I got hooked on running the mile, and, swayed by a persistent and impactful track coach, I eventually left soccer behind to join the cross-country team. My first period arrived right before my first track season; however, while the training cycles progressed, my menstrual cycle didn’t—my second period wouldn’t come until five months later.

Throughout my years on the high school cross-country team, this irregular pattern stuck: I only got about four periods a year and never knew when they would arrive. I felt confused and left out whenever my teammates asked me for a menstrual pad I had no use for, like my body couldn’t do what it was supposed to do.

When it came to running, though, my body felt strong, capable of carrying me through interval workouts and lifting heavy weights during weight room sessions. On the track, I felt more equal to my teammates. The training cycle was one I could control.

At my yearly physical exams, I expressed concern that my periods weren’t occurring monthly, and the feedback was the same every time: I was still young, and sometimes it takes time to become regular. That I accepted. What didn’t sit well with me was what followed: “You’re missing periods because you run a lot. Try eating more.”

Neither felt like an answer to the problem. My 20-something-mile weeks kept me physically fit and helped me deal with anxiety, especially when my dysfunctional home life felt out of control. Not only did the exam show I kept a healthy weight, I had been putting on muscle mass from deadlifting 200 pounds. But hoping the doctor was right, I took a year off from distance training.

At 19, I started seeing a new primary care physician. My doctor was surprised when I recounted my prior experiences. “So you’ve never had any blood tests done?” they asked. I underwent the test and a pelvic ultrasound, and it didn’t take very long to get an answer: The likely culprit was polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).

PCOS is the most common endocrine disorder in people assigned female at birth of reproductive age, yet so much about the condition is still unknown, including the cause of PCOS, according to the American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology. The National Institutes of Health requires only two of the following symptoms for PCOS diagnosis (all of which I’ve experienced): ovulatory dysfunction (irregular, heavy, or missed periods), high androgen levels (often manifesting as excessive body hair or acne), and/or one or more cysts on the ovaries. Besides irregular menstruation, PCOS can cause, for example, infertility and weight gain. Although there isn’t a permanent cure, some patients are able to treat their symptoms by managing their lifestyle: eating well, exercising regularly, and getting enough sleep.

The diagnosis came at a turbulent time in my life. I was swept up in another cycle: emotional abuse stemming from controlling relationships. I escaped this abuse through schoolwork and decided to take extra classes over the summer so I could graduate from college a year early and find my own place.

But I also got back to running, which has always helped me build a sense of agency and played a big role in my postgrad transition—I spent that summer running across the empty campus and habitually relying on a few miles to calm me when faced with chaos. I started taking an herbal supplement that others with PCOS raved about. I moved in with roommates. I found a therapist to help me unpack the trauma I’ve experienced.

And at 21, I finally started to get a regular monthly period.

Every menstruation since has felt like Christmas morning…followed by some gnawing cramps.

What I am only now starting to understand is just how much my environment affected my mental health and how that in turn impacted my physical health. I recently read research studies linking PCOS and emotional abuse, and that’s when I found what felt like the last missing link.

I still mourn for the runner I was in high school, who felt lost and frustrated without any answers, dealing with conflicting feelings around her body image. I remember lying on cold, uncomfortable tables, intimidated by informational pamphlets—none of which covered hormonal health—all while doctors were delivering confusing medical advice or dismissing my concerns with oversimplified notions. A 2022 health survey found that 29 percent of women and 21 percent of men felt doctors disregarded their worries during visits. I was told my problem existed “because I ran.” In reality, it’s far more complex than what many people are told, and I am just one example.

I’ve since run two half marathons while maintaining regular periods throughout each training cycle. Running was never the problem. On the contrary, the very thing doctors blamed my symptoms on brought me relief all along—and I will never give it up again.

Kristine Kearns, a writer and avid runner, joined Runner’s World and Bicycling in July 2024. She previously coached high school girls cross country and currently competes in seasonal races, with more than six years of distance training and an affinity for weightlifting. You can find her wearing purple, baking cupcakes, and visiting her local farmers market.

#8770. The 10 Best Hats for Runners Who Hate Visors and Headbands

A running hat shields your eyes and tames flyaway hair. These are our editors’ top picks. Plus some winter beanies to help keep you warm.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Editor’s Note, November 20, 2026: There are several markdowns on our list for Black Friday! The hi-vis and reflective Headsweats Cap and Nathan Run Cool Stash Hat are both 25% off. Scroll down for even more hats on sale!

You won’t catch me heading out for a run without a hat. Unlike headbands, which tend to slip over my eyes or off my head, caps stay put and have a long list of features that optimize your run. The whole point of a hat is to make my runs easier.

When I’m shopping for the perfect hat, it has to check off several boxes:

The hat completes my race outfit when I’m running any distance from a mile to a marathon. It keeps my hair from getting into my eyes, and sometimes has extra features, like UPF or even a pocket. And with brands making hats with cool patterns, it can also be a vessel for self-expression. They know that wearing a favorite accessory, one that puts the fun in functionality, can get you into the right headspace when you run.

I started wearing running hats seven years ago. I’m so used to wearing a hat on a run that I feel naked running without one. As I accumulated hats, I started to see some fits and features trumped others. The hats on this list were evaluated with years of experience, research, and hat testing.

On top of my own research, I also had some of our RW staffers test caps and provide feedback.

The caps below all have features that cater to different needs and types of runs. From logging a run on a blistering hot day, going for a workout in the evening, or having a penchant for snacking on pickles during training, know this: there’s a hat for that.

I’ve also added some beanies for the colder months. When testing beanies, I paid attention to fit, comfort, and warmth. It’s not true that you’ll catch cold if your head isn’t covered, but that doesn’t mean you shouldn’t wear a hat to keep your cool.

The Ciele FSTCap wins Best Overall as a cap-wearing runner because of its no-fuss, flexible design. The brim isn’t rigid, allowing it to sit comfortably on your head, and it doesn’t flop out of shape. It’s lightweight and breathable, with fast-drying, anti-odor mesh panels.

But its best feature is the adjustable bungee cord closure. I’ve worn several iterations of Ciele FSTCap at races, and the simplicity of the hat gives me peace of mind before racing because the toggle doesn’t require much dexterity when my arms feel like Jell-O during a marathon when I have to loosen or tighten the cord. It’s machine-washable, too.

This hat is Best Budget, but it’s also Best Visibility. The entire rim of this Headsweats’s Hat has reflective trim for visibility in low light, making a car’s lights heighten your bobbing cap’s outline when you’re running on the shoulder at dusk or dawn, or even nighttime. This feature is fantastic if you feel the neon colors are a little too loud to your liking. The black version isn’t a bad choice, thanks to the reflective rim.

The hat is a great tool when you’re an early riser or night owl, and the knit shell is soft and breathable. I do have one main critique: it looks cheaply made. I can get over the knit material wearing fast—proper care, like machine washing and air-drying only, should add to the cap’s longevity. Maybe it’s the lack of patterns or even mesh panels or overlays besides the logo on the side. While this hat doesn’t win fashion contests, it definitely fulfills its purpose for running safely by staying visible.

The Ponyflo Alex Active was tested by me and editor Monique LeBrun, who said we should add this hat to our guide for runners who specifically wear high hairstyles. The positioning of the pony opening allows you to run without your visor comically almost covering your eyes if your hair is half-braided high. Runners like me will appreciate how the positioning makes my hair stop just above my back so it’s not whipping my back when I run.

The hat comes in a variety of colors and there’s even an edition with a longer, wider brim for more sun coverage; though both LeBrun and I felt like we were about to spend a day out gardening wearing them. We felt the brim on the Alex Active sufficed, but the option is there.

Even though the Ciele FSTCap is my racing hat of choice, we’re giving the best racing hat accolade to the Rnnr Pacer Hat. Our testers loved how feather-light the Pacer is and how its perforated panels provide ultimate ventilation.

My one knock would be the buckle, but we didn’t find ourselves struggling to adjust the closure.

“I suppose the best thing I can say about this hat is that never once did I have to adjust it midrun,” said RW News Director Andrew Daniels, who tested the whimsically graphic Jungalow version.

Our other Pacer tester, News Editor Theo Kahler, chose to wear the less loud, mostly black Bolt iteration. He appreciated how the hat wasn’t bulky or stiff. “It didn’t give me headaches like some hats do,” he said. But he had one complaint: “On the inside, it says ‘Party pace wins the race.’ I don’t really know what that means and could personally do without that.” And as Scroogy as the comment may have sounded, I got a kick out of that.

A pocket in a hat is hard to find, so I was glad to stumble across Nathan’s Run Cool Stash. The hidden pocket can doubly serve as storage space for ice, a key, or even an ID card. The pocket is drop-in below and above; I can tuck in my ID card in both flaps, or clip on a running light. It’s a close stretch against your head so items won’t bounce in the compartment as you run. It’s perfect for my key fob when I park my car by a trail, and can’t store it in my pocket-free shorts.

One caveat: you can only stash on one side of the hat, so if you’re feeling the heat on your right side, I guess you’ll have to wear the cap backwards to cool that side down.

All hail the hard-brimmed trucker hat—only Oiselle does theirs with a twist. The firm brim folds in half down the center, making it easy to downsize into a little triangle and stash into your pocket if you want the sun to hit your face (or maybe have that hat rim forehead imprint fade before you head to work in the morning).

This was the only hat I packed when I stayed in Sydney for a week leading up to the marathon. The interior sweatband’s mantra “Go fast, take chances” was the positive energy I needed running a race on the opposite side of the world. The wide-holed mesh back also kept my head cool as the race went on and the day got warmer.

A small drawback is how funky the hat can get after a couple wears. The hat is hand-wash only, which explains why an old Runner Trucker’s toggle broke after a machine wash. The hat is mighty on the run, but delicate during a wash cycle.

I’m going on five years running in my Pickle Peeps hat and have had several compliments over the years whenever I wore it. The all-over print of smiling, shades-wearing dills, gherkins, and cornichons helps me take my races not too seriously. And I’ll absolutely use this hat as an unvoiced request to have the pickle that comes with your sandwich during a postrun brunch.

I loved this hat so much, I called a Barnes & Noble in Dallas, Texas, to find it and please mail it back when I realized I returned home without my Pickle Peeps in tow. But it’s not just this hat: bananas, ice cream, flying pigs, pizza slices—I have a Sprints hat for every craving and every mood.

My only critique is the Velcro closure. It’s ruined running shirts, scarves, and whatever else is in my laundry basket or accessories pile. Sprints has snapbacks, but they don’t come in an extensive pattern collection. Sometimes I have to safety-pin the closure when the humidity puffs out my hair.

The Varsity Runner’s Hat brings to mind snowy winters on campus when I went to college in New England. The hat stays put when I head out on windy winter runs, and functions as an out-and-about beanie when I’m not running. The 100-percent merino wool material helps with thermoregulation and sweat-wicking.

The Creek Run Beanie’s waffle knit texture screams cozy, but you can also wear it when you’re actually running (as its name suggests), or skiing if that’s also your thing during the winter. This hat is stretchy but it does run small.

The Skida Alpine is a stretchy, toasty hat that doesn’t overheat your head. Senior Editor Cat Bowen appreciated how the hat was sensory-friendly; its material feels super smooth, and it requires no tugging or micro-adjusting.

Fit can sometimes be tricky when the hat you’re interested in is unisex, or the over-confidently phrased “one size fits all.” You want the hat to be secure around your head so it doesn’t fly off on windy runs, but not too tight that you get a headache.

If the hat comes in multiple sizes, peruse the site’s fit instructions to match. If it’s the dreaded OSFA, check the type of adjustability and material to make sure it stretches and it can expand—or tighten—around your crown.

Concerning caps, you have plenty of options to consider in terms of adjustability and closures. Velcro allows you to easily adjust without fumbling with toggles or buckles and straps, but the material isn’t stretchy and can lose its adhesiveness. Buckles/snaps stay put but can be a pain to troubleshoot and aren’t always easy to adjust midrun.

My personal favorite is the bungee toggle, but they don’t always lock in place and the cord can overstretch over time.

I’m the owner of several hats and no matter how much I rotate or wash them, they eventually get funky. Besides retiring old hats or soaking them in vinegar and baking soda, one thing that doesn’t draw flies to my head postrun is perforated panels or mesh on my cap.

Material is also key, especially when it comes to beanies. Instead of the inevitable sauna your head would be subjected to running in a rigid, cotton-canvas trucker hat, technical running caps are made of nylon and polyester, and beanies are made of polyester and merino wool, which evaporate moisture by drying fast.

Any ol’ running hat, IMHO, is better than none, but there are hats with extra features to look for if you want a hat more tailored to your needs. Some hats come with UPF to block UVB and UVA rays. Reflective detail is something to consider if your runs are mostly in low light. Pockets are great for storing small items, like a key or even a photo ID if you’re okay with running with a noticeable rectangle on the side of your head. I sure am.

How do I measure my head to get my hat size?

The circumference around your head, above your eyebrows and ears is the measurement you seek. You can use a tape measure, or string and ruler if you don’t have measuring tape, to find your circumference. Then, check the brand’s sizing, if provided, to find your fit.

This depends on the thinness of the material and the breathability features—is it mesh, perforated? Some caps like the Nathan Cool Stash Hat can store cold packs or ice in a pocket. An easy way to keep your head cool is to dunk your hat in cold water before heading out on a run. And to keep your head warm? Go with a hat made of merino wool, which naturally insulates.

#8769. The Anti-Movement Core Routine Every Runner Needs

Glute bridge post-run. (Photo: Aleksandr Kondratov, Getty)

For this article, physical therapist Jennie Hansen analyzed a new study on anti-movement vs. dynamic core training and built a simple, science-backed core routine for runners based on the findings. The routine targets the deep stabilizing muscles that protect your spine and improve performance.

“Core strengthening” is a term runners frequently toss around. We all know we need it. But what exactly is it, and what should it entail? (Hint: Not crunches.)

When we talk about the core, we mean the abdominal muscles, low back, gluteal, pelvic, and hip muscles that support the spine and trunk. These muscles include both smaller, deep groups that attach directly to the spine to provide stabilization and larger, more global ones that can assist with stability and produce movement.

Why do we need this area to be strong? Well, even non-runners need to pay attention to their core strength to avoid lower back pain, which is the top cause of years lived with disability. Athletically, the core must create proximal stability to allow for powerful, efficient movements distally—which requires adequate strength combined with coordinated neuromuscular activation and control. So, core strength is certainly important for pain reduction, injury prevention, and athletic performance.

When running, the trunk serves to provide a stable base of support so that the legs can effectively generate the forces that create forward movement. These forces are transferred across the trunk and counterbalanced by the arms, requiring coordination between the hips, trunk muscles, and shoulders.

While running appears to be purely a forward (sagittal plane) activity, the trunk muscles are hard at work controlling side-to-side (frontal plane) and rotational (transverse plane) forces. Muscle activation and timing change with speed, with higher speeds generally requiring more control and work. The deep trunk muscles also contribute to respiration.

While some small trunk motion naturally occurs with running, excessive motion is detrimental. Increased trunk flexion is associated with decreased running economy and increased loading rates and vertical impact forces. Increased lateral trunk lean has also been linked to increased loading rates, which may play a role in the development of certain injuries.

Even though most of us know that crunches are out, there’s still plenty of confusion about how to train our cores. While strength work doesn’t need to look exactly like running, it does need to meet (and exceed) its demands—meaning that stability should be emphasized over motion.

Enter a recent study comparing neuromuscular activation between “anti-movement” and “dynamic” core training. Unlike traditional dynamic core exercises, which work the trunk and spinal musculature by moving through flexion, extension, rotation, and side bending, anti-movement exercises resist external forces, forcing stabilization throughout the trunk—basically, trunk isometrics.

The 12-week study compared a combination of Pallof holds and plank variations (incorporating bands and the TRX suspension trainer for progression) in the anti-movement program against a dynamic program that included exercises such as sit-ups, leg raises, jack knives, Russian twists, windshield wipers, and back extensions (incorporating Swiss balls for progression).

While both exercise groups demonstrated enhancements in neuromuscular efficiency compared to a control group, improvements were overall greater in the anti-movement group, particularly within the deep local musculature that activates prior to limb movement and plays an important role in stabilizing the spine.

The authors therefore hypothesized that this enhanced neuromuscular efficiency could improve endurance, delay fatigue, and reduce the need for recruitment of larger, more global muscles—thus protecting the spine and potentially decreasing injury risk while improving performance.

Runners can apply these findings and consider an “anti-movement”-focused core routine, similar to the one used in the study. Nothing fancy or extensive is required—just one exercise each to resist the trunk’s motions (flexion, extension, rotation, and side-bending/lateral flexion). Simple plank variations and other holds work well to streamline your core routine efficiently and effectively.

Targets: Anti-extension · full core (local and global)

The front plank is a classic core stability exercise that falls into the anti-extension category, challenging most of both the local and global core muscles.

Targets: Anti-flexion · spinal extensors and glutes

While the study used a supine plank as its anti-flexion exercise, the shoulder position required could be a limiter, so bridge holds are likely a more practical way for many runners to work the posterior trunk muscles, including the spinal extensors and gluteals.

Targets: Anti-lateral flexion · lateral trunk and hip muscles

The side plank can be considered an anti-lateral-flexion exercise, challenging the lateral trunk and hip musculature.

Targets: Anti-rotation · obliques and deep abdominal rotators

The Pallof press is a common anti-rotation exercise, challenging the deep abdominal rotators, including the obliques.

#8768. These 10 Editor-Approved E-MTBs Deliver Real Trail Capability

Trail-ready electric mountain bikes for every budget, from hardtails to high-power builds.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Autumn is our favorite season for mountain biking. The air is crisp, the dirt is grippy, and we can’t wait to head to the singletrack after work and on weekends for great rides. And more than ever, like many other mountain bikers, we’re choosing E-MTBs for our rides. Electric mountain bikes help you maximize those rides and spend more time on your favorite trails.

Today’s electric mountain bikes use lightweight motors and batteries, making them super capable and amazingly fun on the trail. And while heavier than traditional mountain bikes, these pedal-assist models allow you to cover more miles, ride faster, and tackle challenging climbs.

E-MTBs are engineered for performance on singletrack trails and deep in the woods. And while their low-power motors provide a boost when pedalling, E-MTBs are not electric motorcycles. You still have to pedal an electric mountain bike; you can’t simply twist a throttle and blast down the trail.

The best E-MTBs blend mountain bike components, suspension, and geometry with electronic technology in a brilliant fashion. Like non-electric mountain bikes, some E-MTBs blur the lines of XC and lightweight trail bikes, while others are burlier and take suspension and geometry cues from the top-performing enduro and downhill racing mountain bikes.

Aventon recently launched the Current, the brand’s first full-suspension E-MTB, and it is a gem! The Current ADV offers incredible value, and it’s trail-ready right out of the box. Trevor Raab, Bicycling’s Senior Photographer and Test Team member, said, “The bike’s intuitive ride feel will please experienced mountain bikers and also benefit first-time mountain bikers. The Current’s motor and interface provide riders with a wide range of tuning options and lots of data.”

The Current ADV features an aluminum frame with 140mm rear wheel travel and a great-feeling motor boasting 750 peak Watts and 110Nm torque. (The Current also has a Boost mode that bumps power to 850W and torque to 120Nm.) Rounding out the ADV are a RockShox Psylo Gold fork, SRAM DB8 brakes, SRAM Eagle 70 Mechanical transmission, and a tubeless wheelset with Maxxis Minion EXO tires.

In his full review of the bike, “Aventon Goes Full Performance: The Current Electric Mountain Bike Is Surprisingly Dialed,” Raab especially likes the Current’s intuitive and easy-to-use interface. It’s loaded with ride data and the ability to tune the motor settings.

Want a carbon frame and electronic drivetrain? The Current EXP is a great package for $5,999.

Specialized’s Turbo motor is a benchmark for electric mountain bike performance. It has plenty of power and torque, and the Morgan Hill, California-based brand has updated, polished, and refined the motor over several years. However, the biggest downside to Specialized E-MTBs has been their very steep starting price. But that has changed.

Specialized’s newest Levo model brings the platform to a more palatable $5,000 price. The Turbo Levo 4 Alloy uses the same motor and battery as the pricier carbon-chassis Expert model but with an aluminum frame, heavier components, and mechanical shifting to save pennies. The brand bolts its 105Nm torque and 810-watt Turbo 3.1 motor to a 150mm-travel, full-suspension aluminum frame and equips the bike with value-packed parts. SRAM brakes, a mechanical drivetrain, and Marzocchi suspension highlight the alloy Levo 4’s component package.

Hardtail mountain bikes are a gateway into the sport for many riders because they’re simple, sturdy, and affordable. Plus, big, burly full-suspension mountain bikes aren’t for everyone. For some riders, they’re overkill—adding cost and complexity without delivering benefits that match their needs. Hardtail E-MTBs provide pedal assistance for about the same price as full-suspension non-electric mountain bikes.

When launched two years ago, the Ramblas impressed me with its great performance and capability for the price—and Aventon’s recent upgrades make it even better on the trail. The revised Ramblas ADV’s trail-forward components include a RockShox Psylo fork with 35mm stanchions, a 1x12 SRAM Eagle drivetrain that can handle most climbs, powerful four-piston SRAM DB6 brakes, and a useful dropper seatpost. The ADV’s tubeless rims and 2.4-inch Maxxis tires are also upgrades. These components are unmatched by any other hardtail E-MTB, especially at this price.

Superlight e-MTBs offer an intriguing compromise: In exchange for a less powerful drive unit, you get a lighter bike that feels and handles more like an analog mountain bike.

With the Turbo Levo R, Specialized asks: What if you didn’t need to compromise?

The Levo R has the same drive unit and battery as the Levo 4, but in a lighter, shorter-travel package with matched 29-inch wheels. It’s around 5 pounds lighter than a standard Levo 4 at the same price. In the top-of-the-line S-Works trim, the DU offers up to 111 Nm of torque and 850 watts of peak power with an 850 or 900Wh battery. The 41.4-pound (18.8 kg) S-Works Ultralight uses a 600Wh battery to save weight. Lower-priced models offer 105 Nm, 810 watts, and an 840Wh battery.

After spending the better part of a year riding an S-Works Levo R (46.7 lb., size S3), senior test editor Matt Phillips calls it a winning combination for many riders. “It has all the capability and range of a big battery and full-power DU, but in a bike that’s much more flickable, lively, and, frankly, easier to ride than a heavier and bigger-travel e-MTB.” He says Specialized’s e-MTB hardware, frames, and suspension are the icing on top, and calls the Levo R one of the most entertaining mountain bikes, powered or unpowered, he’s ridden this year.

The 29-inch-wheeled Cannondale Moterra 4 has a subdued appearance, which makes it a sleeper. Many full-suspension E-MTBs routinely cost more than $10,000. However, Cannondale keeps the Moterra 4 to a more modest $5,500 while still packing a lot of punch for its price.

At the heart of the Moterra is a trusty Bosch Performance Line CX motor mounted on a 150mm-travel aluminum full-suspension frame. And inside the bike’s stout downtube is a 600Wh Bosch battery. Cannondale’s product team made smart component choices—such as the excellent Shimano Cues drivetrain and 160mm-travel SR Suntour Xeron air-sprung fork—that save cost without sacrificing much performance. The Moterra 4 also has a long-travel dropper seatpost, tubeless wheels, and Tektro disc brakes.

If you buy the Moterra 4 through rei.com, you can have it shipped to your nearest REI location for professional assembly with in-store or curbside pickup. You also get one year of free adjustments—or two years if you’re an REI Co-op member.

“I’ve never considered an e-bike a replacement for a traditional bike—until now.” That’s what Matt Phillips said in his review of the excellent S-Works Turbo Levo 4. The latest version of Specialized’s flagship e-MTB is refined, quiet, fun to ride, and refreshingly free of the common annoyances that plague many e-bikes.

Several standout features set the latest S-Works Turbo Levo 4 apart from the crowded E-MTB segment: a powerful motor delivering 111Nm of torque, a larger 900 Wh battery, and the ability to toggle the pedal-assist cutoff between Class 2 (20mph) and Class 3 (28mph). That extra speed might sound excessive, but it’s a welcome boost when you're riding to or between trails.

Though the S-Works Levo 4 is less expensive than its predecessor, it’s still eye-wateringly pricey at $12,500. For better value—relatively speaking—we recommend the Turbo Levo 4 Expert. It offers the same carbon frame, battery, and motor as the pricier model, though with slightly less torque. A 160mm-travel Fox 38 Performance Elite GRIPX2 fork and a Fox Float X Performance Elite shock handle suspension duties, and SRAM’s GX AXS drivetrain handles gear changes.

Salsa’s Moraine 145 costs less than many hardtail E-MTBs, yet it’s packed with value. This dual 29-inch-wheeled trail bike comes equipped with Fazua’s Ride 60 motor (60 Nm of torque) and a 430Wh battery. While it has less torque and a smaller-capacity battery than higher-priced competitors, the Moraine has enough power for some serious fun in the woods and on singletrack.

The frame uses a Split Pivot suspension system designed by Dave Weagle (the mastermind behind the dw-link suspension system used by Pivot), for a balance of performance and pedalability. A 10-speed Shimano Cues drivetrain with four-piston Shimano brakes, a dropper post, and Terravail tubeless tires round out the component selection on this feature-packed full-suspension E-MTB.

One advantage of an e-MTB is climbing faster and with less effort, leaving you fresher for the descent. A long-travel bike helps you make the most of that on steep, rough trails. It’s like having a personal chairlift for lapping downhill trails.

Cannondale’s Moterra Carbon LT 2 pairs a Bosch Performance Line CX motor and 750Wh battery with 165mm of plush, coil-sprung rear travel and a 170mm fork. Its frame combines a carbon front triangle with an alloy swingarm. Size-specific suspension kinematics tailor the suspension performance to each frame size. The mullet setup pairs a 29-inch front wheel with a 27.5-inch rear, giving you more room to move behind the saddle on steep terrain while keeping the larger front wheel’s rollover advantage. The battery is removable for off-bike charging.

For riders who prioritize steep descents and the refinement and reliability of a Bosch drive unit, the Moterra LT 2 is a strong choice.

It’s no exaggeration to say Avinox reshaped the performance e-MTB market. Developed and launched by drone maker DJI before becoming an independent company, Avinox set new benchmarks with the M1: 105 Nm of torque and up to 1,000 watts of peak power. It also matched or exceeded established brands in features, function, and assist performance. Suddenly, longtime players were off the back, some way off the back.

Before they could catch up, Avinox followed the M1 with the more powerful, refined M2S: up to 150 Nm of torque and 1,500 watts of peak power. But power isn’t the whole story. Senior features director Louis Mazzante says the M2S “isn’t the thunderously loud, chassis-shaking hot-rod motor that its power suggests. It is quiet. It’s smooth. It’s refined.” He also praises its feature-packed, easy-to-use app and touch-screen controls, and says the motor’s power is smooth and tractable.

That blend of power, control, and features has made the M2S highly desirable to bike brands. Ari’s Wire Peak 3.0 stands out as an affordable way to get it.

Starting at $4,999, the Wire Peak pairs the M2S with an 800Wh battery in an aluminum frame with 150mm of rear travel and a 160mm fork. This setup delivers up to 150 Nm of torque in Boost mode and 1,300 watts of peak power. The bike also has a four-bar suspension design, 29-inch or mullet wheel compatibility, and independent high/low and long/short geometry adjustments.

Ari delivers each bike directly to the buyer with a rider-specific setup. Buyers can customize the build through the configurator, and Ari will accommodate most off-menu parts and upgrade requests.

After his first rides on his long-term test bike, senior test editor Matt Phillips called the chassis excellent, Ari’s buying process superb, and the drive unit best in class. He says the Wire Peak would be his choice if he were buying an e-MTB today.

The DRT 1.1 (from REI’s in-house Co-Op Cycles brand) is a good pick if you’re looking for an electric mountain bike to explore mellower trails and ride around town. REI equips the bikes with a dependable Bosch Performance Line mid-drive motor and internal battery.

This hardtail rolls on tubeless-compatible 27.5-inch wheels with 2.6-inch-wide Maxxis Rekon tires for off-road capability. The DRT’s 100mm-travel SR Suntour fork with thru axle isn’t glamorous, but it works. The only notable component missing is a dropper seatpost; it would enhance the bike’s trail capability and help riders feel more confident on challenging terrain.

Traditional analog mountain bikes are usually grouped by frame travel. E-MTBs, on the other hand, are categorized by their power. However, more power ≠ more better. Pick the style that suits your riding needs, budget, and local trail access.

⚡️ Full-Power E-MTBs are the most common style and are generally equipped with roughly 750-watt peak power (1 horsepower) and 85 torque, or more. Bosch, Shimano, and Specialized are three commonly used motor brands for these bikes.

⚡️ Lightweight E-MTBs feature motors with less power and torque (50 to 60 Nm) and lower-capacity batteries. As a result, these bikes weigh less than other E-MTBs and ride more like an unassisted mountain bike, but with a little help on the climbs. Lightweight electric mountain bikes are less popular now than a couple of years ago, which means you can score good deals on great riding bikes.

⚡️ High-power e-MTBs are the newest category of electric mountain bikes, and they’re quickly becoming one of the year’s most talked-about cycling trends. These motors produce more than 1,000 watts of peak power and 110 Nm of torque. Category leader Avinox’s latest unit delivers an incredible 1,500 watts and 150 Nm of torque. Its power and performance have prompted Bosch and Specialized to respond with firmware updates that boost the torque and power of their premium drive units. Even so, the Avinox remains the most powerful drive unit available. But high-power motors aren’t without detractors, or potential consequences. Their use has sparked debate and hand-wringing in the mountain biking community over how much power is too much. Remember: “With great power comes great responsibility.”

When you’re shopping for an electric mountain bike, you must factor in not only the motor’s power and features, but also the bike’s basic capabilities.

Since electronic mountain bikes are heavier than non-motorized bikes, you’ll want to consider a bike with more suspension travel than you have on your non-motorized bike. The longer your travel, the more cushion you’ll get when you encounter obstacles.

Most full suspension E-MTBs are in the 150- to 160mm travel range, which offers a nice balance of increased comfort and improved control for first-time buyers.

There are three electric-assist classes available in the United States, and the use of each class of bike can vary by state, city, and area you are riding. Be sure to check local regulations before buying and before riding on trail systems.

Class 1 motors kick in only when you pedal and stop helping you at 20 mph. Class 2 also offers pedal assist up to 20 mph, but these bikes can also have a throttle-powered mode that allows users to engage the motor without pedaling. Class 3 is pedal-assist like Class 1, but helps you until you reach 28 mph.

Class 1: 20 mph max assist speed; throttle is not standard equipment.

Class 2: 20 mph max assist speed; throttle comes standard equipment.

Class 3: 28 mph max assist speed; throttle is not standard equipment

Other countries classify e-bikes differently, and many countries do not allow e-bikes to assist riders beyond 20 miles per hour.

Most performance-oriented electric mountain bikes are Class 1. Electric mountain bikes generally feature one of two types of motors: mid-drive motors, which are contained in the frame at the bottom of the bike between the pedals; and rear hub motors, which are built into the rear wheel.

Bikes with rear hub motors are generally less expensive but are also less powerful. A mid-drive motor will almost always offer more power. Because the extra weight on a mid-mount bike is centered in the bike and lower to the ground, these bikes are generally easier to handle than bikes with hub motors. Mid-mount bikes do tend to be more expensive, but all of our favorite bikes feature this type of motor.

Battery Life, Range, Maintenance, and Safety

On top of the motor, you’ll want to consider the battery size and range. More is always better for performance, but a battery with a longer range will also weigh more and cost more.

As a bike's weight increases, it requires more effort from the rider to handle. This is especially an important consideration for smaller riders; extra weight can also become a bigger challenge at faster speeds, when you need to ride the bike more aggressively.

A lighter bike will offer better handling, but if you sacrifice too much battery capacity to cut weight, you may find yourself pedaling home with no assist if you take a wrong turn.

Like all e-bikes, E-MTBs can be pedaled as a normal bike if the battery dies, so you’ll still be able to get home, but it will require extra effort and possibly more time.

While we can confidently say a larger battery provides more range, it is difficult to accurately estimate any e-bike's exact range. Many factors impact an e-bike's range: How much boost you’re using (most power systems offer three or four settings), how much you weigh, the terrain you’re riding, how much climbing you’re doing, the air temperature, rolling resistance from the tires, and even how clean and lubricated the drivetrain is.

Don’t take any brand's word on its range claims. Start conservatively as you test your bike’s range. The more you ride, the better you’ll understand how far your batteries can carry you in different conditions. If your bike’s main battery isn’t cutting it, some models let you add an external range booster or swap the internal battery for a fresh one. Be warned: These accessories can be expensive!

Like all batteries, e-bike batteries do lose capacity every time they’re charged and discharged. Unfortunately, that means that the more you ride, the sooner you’ll need to replace your battery. Even so, an e-bike battery should give you years of reliable riding.

Follow your bike's manufacturer’s recommendations for storage, but most batteries will last longer if stored with about a 40-percent charge (but don’t forget to plug your bike in about six hours before riding, to make sure you start your ride with a full charge).

Batteries should also be stored at room temperature whenever possible and not left outside or in an unheated garage in freezing temperatures. Some bike brands, including Specialized, have a setting that will prevent the battery from charging fully. This feature is designed to extend the battery’s life, but you may want to disable the feature if the rides you regularly take use your battery’s full capacity.

If, after a few years, your battery loses enough capacity that you want to replace it, be sure to contact your bike’s manufacturer or local dealer and purchase a certified replacement battery through the brand or its dealer.

Don’t be tempted by cheaper options available online from third-party brands. These third-party batteries are generally not certified by bike brands and may void your bike’s warranty. More importantly, third-party replacement batteries often do not have important safety features, and, as a result, these batteries have been identified as the cause of several serious fires.

There is currently legislation pending at the state and federal level that will bar the sale of non-certified batteries in the U.S., but they are still available as of this writing.

While a handful of bicycle drivetrain manufacturers exist, almost every e-mountain bike will have either a Shimano or SRAM drivetrain. Both are reputable manufacturers that offer reliable shifting and a wide-ranging gear set. Some drivetrains feature electronic shifting. Such drivetrains offer quick and precise shifting, but they will add cost.

The added power of an e-bike puts more strain on a bike’s drivetrain. You can expect to replace your chain more frequently, but you can get more life out of your components if you back off the pedals when shifting, and ease the chain between gears instead of mashing the shifter and the pedal at the same time.

Given the increased weight of an electronic mountain bike, you’ll want to make sure yours is equipped with hydraulic disc brakes, as most are. These brakes offer lots of stopping power and modulation, which ensures you’ll remain in control regardless of your bike's weight, or how fast you go.

Several brands offer hydraulic disc brakes, though again, Shimano and SRAM usually lead the way. For additional power, look for bikes featuring four-piston brakes.

Bicycling has been reviewing bikes and gear for over 50 years, and our recommendations are grounded in decades of real-world experience. Our test team—Deputy Editor Tara Seplavy, Senior Test Editor Matt Phillips, Test Editor Dan Chabonov, and Senior Photographer Trevor Raab—collectively brings 75-plus years of ride-testing knowledge to every product we evaluate.

For this guide to electric mountain bikes, Matt and Tara led the charge, drawing from their deep category expertise and the team’s hands-on testing across a wide range of terrain and conditions. These picks reflect what we’ve learned through thousands of miles of testing: The E-MTBs that deliver the right mix of price, ride quality, trail capability, and pedal-assist performance. Whether you’re climbing faster, riding farther, or just having more fun, these are the best electric mountain bikes you can buy right now.

With expert instruction from pro rider Chaz Turmon, this program features motivating follow-along video sessions and flexible workouts you can do almost anywhere to help you ride faster, train smarter, and watch your numbers climb.

This holistic program covers all the tips and tricks needed to improve your riding technique, master cadence, stack speed and endurance workouts, build strength off the bike, and fine‑tune gear in order to achieve the speed gains you dream about.

Watch as host Alison Tetrick takes you through everything you need to know to ride your first (or fastest) century. Along with other cycling experts, she explains how to find the best gear, build endurance, fuel your body during the ride, and much more.

Cycling is the best way to stay fit as you age. With the help of host Peter Abraham and other experts, you’ll learn everything you need to get started and stay riding into your golden years, including choosing a bike, finding a plan, and optimizing recovery.

Whether you’re constantly feeling aches or you want to maximize your performance gains, you need the right bike fit. With this guide, host Jenna Foley and certified bike fitter Jonathan Blyer walk you through the process and offer up DIY tips.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

A gear editor for his entire career, Matt’s journey to becoming a leading cycling tech journalist started in 1995, and he’s been at it ever since; likely riding more cycling equipment than anyone on the planet along the way. Previous to his time with Bicycling, Matt worked in bike shops as a service manager, mechanic, and sales person. Based in Durango, Colorado, he enjoys riding and testing any and all kinds of bikes, so you’re just as likely to see him on a road bike dressed in Lycra at a Tuesday night worlds ride as you are to find him dressed in a full face helmet and pads riding a bike park on an enduro bike. He doesn’t race often, but he’s game for anything; having entered road races, criteriums, trials competitions, dual slalom, downhill races, enduros, stage races, short track, time trials, and gran fondos. Next up on his to-do list: a multi day bikepacking trip, and an e-bike race.

## Flying Business Class Across Two Continents for the Price of One Imagine settling into a fully flat bed on a Boeing 787-9 somewhere over the Pacific, a warm towel in your hand, Japan behind you and Singapore ahead. You've already spent three days eating ramen in Tokyo — a stopover you added to your award ticket for a mere 5,000 extra points. This isn't a once-in-a-lifetime splurge. This is what the ChooseFI community calls a **nearly free** trip, engineered through one of the most underappreciated sweet spots in the entire travel rewards ecosystem. The Air Canada Aeroplan stopover rule is genuinely one of the last great loopholes in loyalty travel. Here's the math that makes your jaw drop: a business class flight from Toronto to Singapore — routed through Tokyo with a multi-day stopover — retails for **$8,000 to $10,000 in cash**. You can book that same itinerary for **70,000 Aeroplan points** (plus 5,000 for the stopover, so 75,000 total). At a conservative cash value of $8,000, you're extracting **10.7 cents per point** — more than double what most programs offer, and squarely within Aeroplan's documented range of **5.7 to 14.3 cents per point**. To put that in FI terms: if you value your points at even the low end of that range — 5.7 cents per point — 75,000 Aeroplan points are worth **$4,275 in travel**. At the high end, you're looking at **$10,725**. That's a portfolio-level return on the credit card spending and transfer partners you've already been accumulating. What makes this feel different from other premium redemptions is the *shape* of the trip itself. You're not just flying business class — you're building a mini round-the-world itinerary. Tokyo and Singapore in the same award ticket. Two of the world's great cities. Two business class flights. One redemption. The inefficiency here isn't accidental — it's baked into how Aeroplan prices stopovers at a flat 5,000 miles, regardless of where you stop. The program is essentially inviting you to stack experiences on a single award, and the ChooseFI community is the group paying close enough attention to accept that invitation.

The core insight is this: Air Canada Aeroplan uses a fixed partner award chart for Star Alliance flights, and it prices stopovers at a flat 5,000-mile premium regardless of routing complexity. That single policy decision transforms a standard business class award into a multi-destination adventure at a fraction of the combined retail cost.

Here's the mechanism. When Aeroplan relaunched in 2020, it did something most programs had abandoned years earlier: it kept a fixed-rate award chart for partner airlines. While programs like United MileagePlus moved to fully dynamic pricing — where award costs fluctuate with demand — Aeroplan locked in predictable rates for Star Alliance partners. The YYZ to SIN corridor in business class sits at a rate that reflects the geography, not the current demand spike or revenue management algorithm. That's the pricing inefficiency the ChooseFI community can systematically exploit.

Layer on top of that the stopover rule: Aeroplan allows one free stopover on one-way partner awards for just 5,000 additional miles. A stopover is defined as a connection of more than 24 hours. So your Toronto → Tokyo → Singapore routing becomes a Toronto → Tokyo (stopover 3 days) → Singapore itinerary, all on one award ticket, for 75,000 points total. You've essentially purchased two separate international business class flights for the price of one, plus a nominal surcharge.

The other critical piece: Aeroplan charges zero fuel surcharges on partner awards. This was a deliberate policy decision in the 2020 relaunch and it's a massive advantage. Programs like British Airways Avios and Singapore KrisFlyer can add $500–$1,500 in surcharges to long-haul business class awards. With Aeroplan, you pay government taxes only — typically $50–$150 on most itineraries.

You don't need to fly Air Canada or hold an Air Canada credit card to access this. Aeroplan accepts transfers from several major flexible currency programs at a 1:1 ratio:

Chase Ultimate Rewards is your best friend here because transfers are instant, which matters when you're racing to book a specific award seat before someone else claims it. If you hold a Chase Sapphire Preferred, Chase Sapphire Reserve, or Ink Business Preferred, your UR points can become Aeroplan points in seconds.

The booking window is 355 days out, which gives you nearly a full year of planning runway — a significant advantage for families coordinating schedules or travelers targeting peak periods in Tokyo or Singapore. Partner award availability on Aeroplan is generally solid for the Star Alliance network, with business class seats on ANA, Japan Airlines (where applicable), and Singapore Airlines routes opening up regularly. Availability scores a 4 out of 5 for this sweet spot, which reflects genuine accessibility rather than theoretical possibility.

Free calculator shows when you could reach financial independence — plus a savings rate tracker, expense audit, and more.

Never transfer points until you have confirmed, bookable award space in hand. Go to aeroplan.com and use the flight search tool. Select "Business" class, enter your origin and destination (e.g., Toronto YYZ to Singapore SIN), and search for one-way awards. Aeroplan's search engine will show you available partner space directly — you don't need a separate search on partner airline websites, though checking ana.co.jp or singaporeair.com for business class availability can help you triangulate what's open before logging into Aeroplan.

Look for awards showing Star Alliance partner carriers (ANA, Singapore Airlines, and others depending on routing). The system will display the points cost and any routing options. Aeroplan's booking window opens 355 days in advance, so set a calendar reminder to search the moment your target travel window becomes available.

Once you've found an outbound flight you like (e.g., Toronto → Tokyo), call Aeroplan at 1-800-361-5373 or use the online multi-city search to add a stopover at your midpoint city. A stopover is any connection exceeding 24 hours. The system will add 5,000 points to your base award cost. Confirm the full itinerary shows both the Tokyo stopover segment and the onward Tokyo → Singapore flight in the cabin class you want.

Note: Online booking for complex multi-city awards with stopovers sometimes requires a phone call to complete. Budget 30–45 minutes for the call and have your routing clearly written out before you dial.

Determine which flexible currency you'll use. If you have Chase Ultimate Rewards, transfer to Aeroplan first — it's instant. Log into your Chase account, navigate to "Transfer to Travel Partners," select Air Canada Aeroplan, and complete the transfer. Points appear in your Aeroplan account immediately.

If using Amex Membership Rewards, Capital One, or Bilt, initiate the transfer and expect a 1–2 day processing window. Have your Aeroplan member number ready. Do NOT transfer until you've confirmed availability in Step 1.

Once your points land in your Aeroplan account, return to aeroplan.com and complete the booking within the same browser session if possible. Pay the government taxes and fees with a credit card that earns rewards on travel purchases. Taxes on a routing like YYZ → NRT → SIN are typically in the $100–$200 range — no fuel surcharges.

After booking, download or screenshot your itinerary confirmation. Verify the cabin class on each segment. Check in on the Aeroplan website 24 hours before each flight and confirm your seat assignments. For the stopover city, you are responsible for your own accommodation — budget accordingly, and consider this the best "forced layover" you'll ever take.

A stopover is a deliberate break in your journey at a connecting city, where you stay for more than 24 hours before continuing to your final destination. Most loyalty programs treat stopovers as separate tickets, requiring you to pay miles for each segment independently. Aeroplan breaks this convention by allowing one free stopover on one-way awards, meaning your connecting city becomes a bonus destination at zero additional mileage cost. For example, a flight from New York to Tokyo with a 5-day stopover in Istanbul costs the same 75,000 Aeroplan points as flying directly — but you get to explore Istanbul for nearly a week as part of the trip. The stopover must be at a connection point that makes geographic sense for your routing, but with 26+ Star Alliance airlines and hundreds of hub cities, the options are vast.

The Tokyo stopover is yours to explore however you like. Then Singapore Airlines' Business Class on the NRT–SIN leg offers its own benchmark product — a refined seat, excellent service, and arrival into Changi, consistently ranked the world's best airport.
