#8692. Tonal Review (2025): Our Experts Put the Smart Home Gym to the Test

The high-tech home workout system provides a whole-body exercise program.

Written by Stephen Sheehan, CPT × The Expert Panel is a network of specialized health and fitness professionals who help ensure we present the most accurate information to our readers. This includes physicians, certified trainers, elite-level coaches, and more. Learn more about our experts. expert-verified Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC Last updated on Jan 29, 2025

expert-verified Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC

Tonal is a high-tech smart gym that makes starting an effective strength workout as easy as stepping into the next room. It has a cable resistance system with multiple attachments, so there is no need for additional equipment. You can choose between instructor-led sessions or work out independently using the demonstrations on the large touchscreen. There are a variety of workouts outside of strength training, including high-intensity interval training (HIIT), cardio, dance, yoga, Pilates, and more.

As a certified personal trainer and wellness product reviewer, I’ve tried (and stopped using) several pieces of home gym equipment. I also work with a team of other expert product reviewers, some of whom have had Tonal for several years and still use it consistently.

This Tonal review describes our experience using it, including details about the equipment, workouts, accessories, and other features. We also spoke to fitness expert Rachael Gonzalez, C.P.T., C.S.C.S., about Tonal’s workout modes and how they can benefit exercisers.

Based on our experience, we give Tonal an overall 5/5 rating. The only category where it didn’t receive a score is assembly, which doesn’t apply since professional installation is required.

Here’s a look at the scoring breakdown on a scale of 1–5:

We’re extremely satisfied with the Tonal equipment and programming. We can get a full workout without taking up a lot of space with free weights or having to pay to go to a gym and leave the house.

The equipment is durable, and we haven’t had any issues. However, moving the arms can be noisy, which may concern people installing it on a shared wall. We had one arm that clicked slightly for a while, but following the troubleshooting instructions on the Tonal website helped fix it.

Some weightlifting moves don’t feel entirely safe or stable, so we usually replace them with ones we’re more comfortable with. The handles, bar, and rope accessories are comfortable to hold and easy to use.

Tonal automatically adjusts weight as you progress, which is really nice. Some workouts have a movement replacement option where you select a modification for the recommended exercise, which has been helpful in certain instances. For example, during pregnancy, you’re supposed to avoid twisting moves, so when one of our testers started lifting after her first trimester, she could easily substitute these moves.

Tonal has worked very well, and one of our testers says it has drastically improved her strength. When she started using Tonal in 2021, she was in the bottom 25 percent of all women. Now, she’s in the top 28 percent, and watching her score increase has motivated her to keep improving.

The Tonal machine is a wall-mounted smart mirror with a built-in touchscreen and two adjustable arms that extend from the sides of the machine and can be moved up and down depending on what exercises you’re doing. You can choose between an on-demand or live instructor-led class or do your own exercises using the Free Lift option. Throughout each class and in Free Lift mode, a trainer explains how to adjust the arms and attach accessories and demonstrates proper form.

Workouts on the built-in workout app include weightlifting exercises such as squats, deadlifts, shoulder presses, lat pulldowns, tricep extensions, curls, and bench presses. The movement library has over 170 exercises to choose from. Each exercise is performed under the resistance of a cable pulley system using a bar, rope, or handle attachment, with up to 100 pounds of resistance per side for a combined 200 pounds.

Tonal recommends weights for each session based on an initial assessment, and your progress and performance determine adjustments. It offers unique weight modes, video form feedback, and floor workouts such as yoga and Pilates. The Tonal app also gives you access to workouts that don’t require the machine arms, so you can work out on the go.

Tonal uses artificial intelligence—Coach AI—to track progress, movement, and data from your workouts to make adjustments, weight recommendations, program suggestions, and more. You don’t have to worry about answering questions like: What do I need to work on today? What weights should I use? Should I focus on my lower body or do a full-body workout? Instead, one tap of the 24-inch touchscreen reveals an interactive library of on-demand and live classes or workout programs. Even in Free Lift mode, an option often used by experienced lifters, Coach AI tracks your data and makes adjustments and weight recommendations.

The first time you use Tonal, you’ll complete the Strength Assessment, which starts by choosing from the following goals:

After selecting your goal, you’ll indicate whether you are a beginner, intermediate, or advanced exerciser and perform several movements—including a seated lat pulldown, seated overhead press, bench press, and neutral grip deadlifts—to help Coach AI get to know you and adapt to your needs, much like an online personal trainer. Your strength assessment results are used by Coach AI as a baseline when selecting the weight for each movement and to recommend workouts and programs.

While this is a good starting point, it could be better. It’s hard to assess your overall fitness based on a single workout—what if you had an off day? Tonal addresses this by learning more about your strength level based on your performance in subsequent workouts and adjusting the weight settings to reflect your strength better.

During daily training sessions, it uses metrics such as time under tension, power output, range of motion, weight, and time to make weight adjustments and measure progress. Coach AI can detect when your form isn’t correct using your positioning, range of motion, and pacing. If it senses uncertain quality, it provides audible and on-screen reminders and feedback or turns off the weight. For example, the resistance shuts off if the bar tilts during a bench press because it suggests the movement is incorrect or unstable. If it senses you are moving the weight too easily, it increases the load each rep so you get the intended stimulus of the workout.

Another impressive feature is the four weight modes: Spotter, Burnout, Chains, and Eccentric. In Spotter mode, Tonal senses when you are struggling with a rep, lowers the weight so you can complete it, and returns the weight for the next rep to re-challenge your strength. Burnout senses fatigue and reduces weight until you finish the set. The Chains mode replicates the feeling of putting chains on the barbell by increasing the resistance during a lift’s concentric or shortening phase. Eccentric increases the resistance as you release the weight for more time under tension, which may help muscle growth.

Tonal enables each mode automatically during live and on-demand workouts. This automation creates a seamless transition between segments like supersets, where you concentrate on opposing muscle groups with little rest in between. If you want to work out with a partner, weight adjustments for both parties are automated.

Experienced experts lead each workout by demonstrating and talking you through set up and proper form. Even if you choose to follow the Free Lift setting or build a custom workout using the extensive movement library, there are video explanations of how to perform each movement. When you enable a specific weight mode, the weight is adjusted automatically, or you can adjust it manually on the screen using the dial. Interestingly, you can adjust the weight in one-pound increments, an uncommon feature in most cable machines and free weights, which typically adjust in 2.5 or five-pound increments.

To access these features, you’ll need a paid membership for $60 monthly, and Tonal requires a subscription for the first year. The only way to use Tonal without the membership is to manually set the weights to perform unguided exercises like a cable machine.

The purchase price of $3,995 includes the machine (which includes the touchscreen and arms) and no accessories. Aside from the floor workouts, most workouts use the arms and attachments, so Tonal isn’t usable without them. While you can use attachments from other brands, you’ll need to purchase T-lock adapters from Tonal for $43.

The smart accessories bundle from Tonal costs $495. If your budget allows, I recommend buying it because it includes everything you need to start using your Tonal immediately. Each accessory is available separately, so you can also choose what works best for you. Here’s a breakdown of what the bundle includes and pricing for each item individually:

The smart accessories have a safety feature to turn the weight on and off with a button rather than by touching the screen, so you can position yourself before loading. The handles have a button on the side that’s easy to reach while gripping, and the rope and bar come with an attachable clip.

As a beginner, our tester initially thought working out with Tonal was intimidating, but it’s a simple process once you learn how the smart home gym works. With a membership, you can choose between live and on-demand classes or a progressive program. Based on your Strength Score established in the initial assessment, the recommended weights are set automatically for you.

From there, you follow the trainer’s instructions and on-screen prompts to set the arms and choose the right accessories for each move. Tonal automatically adjusts the weight, counts reps, and provides form feedback as you progress through the workout. There’s even an audible cue when you have two reps left, so you know what to expect if you’re facing away from the machine.

Free Lift allows you to choose from the library of movements and do as many sets and reps as you’d like. Much like the classes, the screen displays your live stats, and you receive a workout summary with your time under tension, range of motion, power output, and total volume lifted.

You can do floor workouts such as cardio, yoga, and barre directly on Tonal or by using the Tonal app on another device.

Strength training is the main draw of Tonal, so most of Tonal’s content focuses on weightlifting and HIIT training with weights. In addition to the four weight modes mentioned earlier, there are two custom modes:

Gonzalez says these options add variety and challenge, enhancing strength gains and training overall. “Diversification in your routine keeps you engaged and introduces new challenges,” she says. “Plus, variation can help you push past a training plateau.”

Trainer-led workouts on Tonal automatically implement these modes depending on the intended stimuli, but you can activate them manually in the settings for any workout. You can adjust the weight at any point during your workout using the dial on the screen.

“When training, I’m always super mindful of how my body feels and take it easy when I need to, so the Recovery Mode option would work well for when you’re sore or just want to move,” Gonzalez says. “I really like the eccentric-focused mode. During the eccentric portion of a rep, the muscle lengthens while under tension,” she says. “The eccentric portion of a lift occurs when you are lowering the weight, moving against the opposing force of gravity, and research shows controlled lengthening of the muscle fibers contributes to overall strength and muscle development.”

In addition, there are several other types of workouts available on Tonal, including:

Tonal has a massive catalog of guided workouts and workout programs and a library of over 200 bodyweight moves to allow you to build custom workouts.

The guided programs range from three to five weeks and focus on goals like improving overall fitness, gaining lean muscle mass, and burning fat. For example, Fundamentally Fit guides you through basic movement patterns, and House of Volume uses progressive overload to build strength. Many users on Reddit recommend Four Weeks to Fat Loss, a combination of resistance training and HIIT to maximize energy output. One says, “Four Weeks to Fat Loss did amazing things to my body composition! Doing that program was when I really started to see a difference in how my clothes fit.”

The smart handles help replicate moves performed with dumbbells and kettlebells, like hammer curls, bicep curls, or goblet squats. The smart rope can copy moves with a rope or chains, like pull-throughs or tricep extensions. Finally, the bar can replicate barbell moves such as deadlifts and bench presses. You can purchase accessories from another brand, but the smart accessories bundle from Tonal has Bluetooth connectivity, so you can press a single button on the accessory to turn the weight on or off.

If you buy third-party accessories, you must purchase T-locks from Tonal to attach them securely. Additionally, you’ll need to turn the weight on and off directly on the touchscreen.

Tonal has a roster of expert instructors based in its New York studio and guest coaches who occasionally provide unique content. These fitness experts have diverse backgrounds, from competitive athletes to sports medicine.

All Tonal-created workouts are instructor-led, so you’ll hear tips about form and safety throughout. Each instructor brings a unique style, personality, and expertise to the table, and Tonal users generally find instructors they prefer. For many, this provides the experience of working with a personal trainer, and several of Tonal’s past and current coaches offer personal training services outside of Tonal. For these reasons, Tonal allows you to filter workouts by instructor.

The Tonal app allows you to access your workout history, create workouts, and do floor workouts directly from your phone. The only thing you can’t do on the Tonal app is weightlifting workouts that require using the resistance cables.

In addition, Tonal connects to several fitness apps, including Apple Health, Google Fit, and Strava. It also syncs with several heart rate monitors using Bluetooth, and you can connect to your Amazon Music or Apple Music account to stream or choose from the 14 stations on Tonal Radio.

Tonal has several features to help keep members engaged with the community and the equipment.

First, there are several achievements you can earn for performing certain types of workouts, working out on holidays or birthdays, or reaching milestones like weekly streaks or 1,000,000 pounds lifted. Your workout summary lists the badges and milestones reached and your progress toward the following milestones. The Total Achievements Card shows how many workouts you’ve finished, the pounds you’ve lifted, and the longest weekly streak you’ve completed. You earn badges by trying a new workout type, training consistently, and working out at a different time of day. These achievements can be shared with friends and family using the mobile app.

The Tonal Leaderboard ranks all active exercisers based on how many days or hours they’ve used Tonal in the last 30 days, so the more you train, the higher you’ll rank.

Your Strength Score increases from the baseline as you get stronger and demonstrate progress during workouts. These improvements are calculated based on your historical workout data and are a huge source of motivation for many Tonal users. Using a percentage-based comparison, you can see how your Strength Score ranks against others, so some friendly competition is involved.

Tonal has a very active social media community if you prefer direct interaction with other members. The brand’s private Facebook community, The Official Tonal Community (OTC), has over 53,000 members and regularly hosts workout challenges and live discussions with Tonal trainers.

Our tester has had Tonal for over two years, and she’s used it consistently the entire time, only stepping away briefly for injury recovery and pregnancy.

Before Tonal, despite being fully aware of the benefits of resistance training, she had no weightlifting experience beyond the occasional half-hearted kettlebell or dumbbell workout.

Tonal takes all the guesswork out of resistance training so you can lift the weights and reap the benefits, which is our favorite thing about it. You don’t have to worry about setting weights, planning workouts, increasing weights or reps, or tracking your progress.

At first, our tester didn’t understand Tonal’s difficulty levels. She thought the Beginner, Intermediate, and Advanced class levels aligned with strength and fitness experience, but they correlate with the technicality of the moves involved. Beginner classes may include heavy weights if recommended by your Strength Score and the algorithm. The “beginner” aspect is that the workout moves are less technical, making effective strength training accessible to those who might typically be considered “casual” fitness enthusiasts.

Our tester says Tonal is a lot of fun. She’s discovered she loves lifting weights, and when she misses a few workouts, she gets antsy about getting started again. Tonal introduced her to barre, a ballet-inspired floor workout she’s grown to adore. There aren’t many new floor workouts, which is sad because she loves the barre and pre/postnatal classes.

Our tester has attended live classes, but she doesn’t very often. Sometimes, she struggles with the pacing for floor/cardio workouts but finds the weightlifting workouts easy to follow. Mostly, she sticks to on-demand workouts because she appreciates the guided warm-up, exercise, and cool-down.

One concern users in the Tonal Facebook community raise is the lead trainer demonstrates the moves during a live workout, which is not true for on-demand classes. These workouts use the lead trainer’s voiceover and cut to another trainer demonstrating the exercises. This inconsistency doesn’t bother us, but some say it disrupts their flow or makes it harder to follow.

The instructors showcase their personalities, and none of the workouts our tester watched seem overly scripted or cheesy. Tonal recently moved their studio from California to New York and replaced the coaching staff. Our reviewer had grown accustomed to the “old” coaches and still gravitates toward their workouts because she likes their calm demeanor. Some coaches have a bubbly, energetic coaching style, and others take a tough-love approach.

These trainers have diverse professional backgrounds to support the workouts they design. For example, when our tester’s doctor cleared her to work out after a knee injury, she found Coach Liz’s workouts helpful because the coach is also a physical therapist.

Our tester completed several of the guided programs and saw consistent strength gains from each program. The programs can get repetitive, though, since many of them repeat the same two or three workouts for the duration of the program.

When our tester started using Tonal, her Strength Score was 133, and she was in one of the lowest percentiles of all female Tonal members. Although her progress has been slow, her Strength Score is now 354, and according to Tonal, she’s stronger than 82 percent of all female users. Something about getting higher and higher in those percentiles is supremely motivating for her. In addition to her soaring strength, she’s experienced improvements in her mobility and range of motion.

The base price of Tonal is $3,995, and the optional smart accessories bundle (which we highly recommend purchasing) is an additional $495. Professional installation, which is required, costs $295. Several users on Reddit report signing a Release of Liability waiver and installing it themselves, but there is no option to remove the installation charge at checkout. Tonal often runs promotions and offers free shipping and installation.

A subscription is required for the first year and costs $60 per month. You can discontinue the membership after one year, but you’ll lose access to many features.

If you purchase Tonal, the optional smart accessories bundle, and the required one-year subscription, the total cost of Tonal within the first year is roughly $5,500 before taxes, not including delivery and installation.

A monthly subscription costs $60 per month and isn’t technically required after you’ve completed your first year of membership.

You can only use Tonal as a cable machine for free lift workouts, and without a membership, you won’t have access to any Tonal content, weight modes, workout or strength data, history, or custom workouts.

The Tonal website says professional installation is required. Before purchasing, you’ll need to complete a survey providing additional information for the installers, such as where to set up Tonal and the stud spacing in your walls.

If they determine you don’t have an appropriate place to install it, there are solutions. The brand offers wide-mount adapter bars and installation kits for metal studs. If you have concerns about where you can have Tonal installed, contact the brand’s customer service team for help. Typically, installation fees are $295, but Tonal occasionally offers free delivery and installation.

If you move, you’ll need to schedule a professional reinstallation. Tonal offers relocation packages for moving homes or simply relocating furniture to another room. Relocation fees range from $300 to $500 plus taxes, depending on your chosen service.

Tonal does not cover damage caused by attempting to install or reinstall the home gym, and if you choose this option, Tonal requests you sign a Release of Liability waiver.

Tonal offers a two-year limited warranty on the trainer and touchscreen, which covers parts, shipping, and labor. The smart accessories have a one-year warranty for parts plus shipping and labor. For such a premium (and expensive) piece of equipment, a five-year warranty on the device would be nice—and more comparable to warranties offered by other premium fitness equipment brands.

Tonal customers have had mixed experiences with customer service. Some say customer service quickly and competently addressed their concerns, while others say they needed more urgency from the customer service team.

The Tonal website has several glowing reviews from its users, many of whom say they have canceled their gym memberships while drastically improving their strength and fitness levels. Several reviewers are excited about their progress and enjoy the objective tracking data from workouts.

Tonal has a 2.⅖ on Trustpilot. Several critical reviews mention installation, maintenance, and customer service issues. Tonal partners with a third-party company for delivery, installation, and repairs, and many concerns center around problems with this specific company rather than Tonal itself. Positive reviews mention the variety of workouts, convenience, and ease of use.

People on Reddit say they work out more frequently with Tonal and enjoy the extra time saved from skipping gym commutes. Several mention the cable resistance feels heavier than free weights, so the maximum poundage is not a limiting factor. One user says they wish to see a floor-based alternative in the future for those who rent or need to move.

Tonal is ideal for people who are interested in weightlifting but need guidance and support to get started and see results. It’s a great fit for athletes and highly active people who want to advance in strength training to support their athletic endeavors and fitness goals.

Likewise, many dedicated weightlifters have switched from using free weights to this comprehensive, versatile system. Tonal is an excellent option if you dislike going to the gym and prefer an all-in-one home gym solution.

Tonal isn’t ideal for people outfitting their home gym on a limited budget. For Tonal’s high price tag, you could buy a complete set of dumbbells or other free weights and other equipment or pay for several years of a gym membership.

Additionally, Tonal likely won’t be a good fit for advanced weight lifters already at or near the maximum of 100 pounds per arm offered for many lifts.

This machine requires adequate space to extend the arms to fully perform all necessary movements. If you live in a small or cramped space, it may not work for you.

Our tester has had Tonal for over two years. Here are some of the criteria she used to evaluate Tonal when she first received it, and which are still very important to her two years later:

Tonal and Peloton are very different but complement one another in several ways. Many Tonal users are also Peloton users since Tonal covers the strength training aspect, while the Peloton bike, treadmill, and rower provide heart-pumping cardio workouts. Each app offers live classes, and the monthly subscription to the Peloton App+ is $24, and Tonal costs $60.

The Peloton App One—$12.99 monthly—houses the brand’s floor workouts and has a much larger and more frequently updated library than the Tonal app. Peloton may work better if you enjoy these classes more than weightlifting. It’s more budget-friendly than Tonal, but Tonal offers a more comprehensive strength training system and programming.

Tempo is a smart strength training system and one of Tonal’s major competitors. It utilizes free weights outfitted with sensors rather than Tonal’s electromagnetic cable system.

The Tempo Move—an equipment package with 16 weight plates ideal for beginner and intermediate use and a 12-month Tempo membership—starts at $963. It’s a more accessible system for people with limited budgets and has advanced features such as rep counting and monitoring form. Tester Jordan Smith, C.P.T., says, “It did a great job counting my reps, but it didn’t always pick up on my form.”

The Tempo Move does not come with a screen, so you have to use your phone or other device, whereas Tonal has a dedicated workout space to stream workouts from an app. The Tempo Studio has a 42-inch display and ranges from $2,963–$4,463, depending on your accessory package.

Tonal can be incredible for your health, providing the structure and convenience needed to start and stick to a strength training routine. The fun programming, smart weight recommendations, and space-saving home gym setup make it a worthwhile investment for anyone interested in increasing their strength and who can fit it wisely into their budget.

Yes, after the first year. The $60/month subscription begins at installation and is mandatory for the first 12 months you own the machine. After one year, you can pause or cancel your subscription, and Tonal functions in “Basic Free Lift” mode, where you guide your own workouts. You can’t access your data analytics, workout content, or dynamic weight modes that provide personal training features.

Choosing between Tonal or free weights is a personal choice. Tonal has some pros: It’s space-saving and sets your weight based on your current strength level. Free weights are less expensive and don’t require an internet connection.

Currently, a Tonal membership costs $60 per month. Without the membership fee, Tonal works similarly to a manual cable machine.

Tonal weight feels up to 26 percent heavier than standard weights, according to one Tonal-affiliated study. The weight generated on Tonal maintains resistance throughout the entire rep, unlike free weights, which can feel lighter due to momentum and working with gravity at specific parts of the rep rather than against it.

No, Tonal is an independent company and is not affiliated with Peloton.

No, Tonal requires a WiFi connection, even if you don’t have a paid Tonal membership.

Tonal smart equipment seamlessly integrates with the base Tonal model. If you wish to use your own exercise equipment, you can purchase special adapters from Tonal.

Stephen is an ISSA-certified personal trainer and nutritionist with an immense passion for health and fitness. A two-time University of Florida graduate and longtime rugby player, he brings more than a decade of strength training experience, plus a diverse writing and editing background. When he’s not creating content or hitting the gym, he enjoys traveling, cooking, and attending music festivals around the world.

#8691. Your Holiday Gift for Every Type of Fitness Enthusiast

From the weight-room goer to the trail runner, Altra has options for all the sporty types on your gift list.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

When it comes to holiday gifts for the runner on your list, here’s the hard truth: No one needs another water bottle or foam roller. Instead, go bold and give shoes. But not just any pair. Choose ones that give their toes more room to move—and could make them a better runner by strengthening their feet.

Altra is famous for its roomy toe box, and here’s why that matters: Research found that wider designs better accommodate the foot’s natural shape than standard running shoes. That extra toe room can reduce stress on the feet and allow a fuller range of motion, reducing the risk of injuries not only in the feet, but also the lower back, hips, knees, and ankles.

Along with its signature Altra Fit (roomy toe box and low drop), Altra offers a model for nearly every fitness enthusiast on your list—including you. Here are some top options.

Chilly mornings, humid evenings, slushy roads—when the daily run is a non-negotiable, there’s no such thing as bad weather, only the wrong shoes. The right ones are the Altra Experience Flow 3 GTX, with a waterproof upper to keep the feet dry and comfy and a grippy outsole for traction on wet surfaces. A low 4mm heel drop with a rocker shape adds a bit of propulsion, so your everyday runner can get more momentum with less effort.

Getting started can feel intimidating for many people, and the sheer breadth of gear choices adds to that overwhelm. Make it easy for the newbie on your holiday list and give the Altra Experience Flow 3, which has quickly become a fan favorite. The Experience Flow 3 is lightweight, bouncy, and stylish, and it also boasts a rocker shape geometry for a smooth heel-to-toe transition

Seasoned runners often have two distinct categories of shoes: Ones for long training days and others for race day. The Altra Torin 9 does both jobs, making it a solid choice for the performance-seeking runner who appreciates the ability to wear the same shoes at any distance and still be comfortable. Responsive and soft, with a grippier outsole than the last version, this shoe combines two types of foam for stability and cushioning. There’s also an updated heel shape for improved fit, a secure midfoot that stays in place mile after mile, and the signature toe box that lets toes move freely. This is Altra’s longstanding, bestselling road shoe for a reason.

Trail running is experiencing a massive surge in popularity, with a recent report showing that U.S. participation has jumped by 57 percent since 2019. That means the trail runner on your list may be new to the sport, even if they’re not new to running. Because trails can be muddy, rocky, and root-laden, they require a specialized shoe like the Altra Experience Wild 3. Extra grippy for outdoor terrain while still being lightweight, the Wild 3 offers a rocker shape geometry and a super-practical GaiterTrap—a built-in attachment system that allows trail gaiters to lock onto the back of the shoe. There’s also room for the toes while still having the secure midfoot for natural movement around all those trail obstacles.

If your giftee has been conquering terrain for years, they’ve probably heard about the Altra Lone Peak 9, the shoe that put Altra on the map for trail running. It’s been Altra’s bestselling trail shoe for over a decade, and each version gets better. This ninth generation has been reengineered for more durability, with a revised midsole foam that offers lighter weight than previous iterations. A roomy toe box, space through the midfoot, ripstop mesh upper for high-mileage performance, and ultrasticky grip in practically all conditions? Legendary.

Many gym goers like to warm up with a treadmill session before transitioning into strength work, and that usually requires a shoe change. Not anymore. The Altra Escalante 5 is the brand’s beloved cross-trainer, and it shifts from running to lifting like a pro athlete. Strength training shoes require less soft arch support and cushioning because their main job is to provide stability rather than to absorb impact. The Escalante 5 has a low stack height, streamlined design, and zero drop. That keeps the feet completely flat, mimicking a natural barefoot position favored by serious lifters, while still providing good lateral support for cross-training and functional workouts.

Packing multiple shoes for a vacation or business trip is about as appealing as trying to sneak liquids past airport security. If your gift recipient is the type who looks for a run soon after stepping off the plane, there’s the Altra FWD VIA 2. Softer and more responsive than the previous version of the model, it also boasts a mesh upper for increased breathability, a roomy toe box, and rocker shape geometry. Whether someone is running through the airport, sightseeing for hours, or putting a workout on the vacay itinerary, this is the perfect travel partner.

Elizabeth Millard is a freelance writer focusing on health, wellness, fitness, and food.

#8690. I Thought I Was Getting Slower Because of Age. Then an Incidental Scan Revealed the Real Problem—and Likely Saved My Life.

A longtime runner reflects on an unexpected diagnosis and the chance to start over.

Last year, a lung scan—ordered even though I’d ground out my last butt decades earlier—incidentally picked up a bulge in my aorta. Because I smoked heavily when I was young, my doctor sent me for a screening after the age eligibility had been lowered, just in case. While the scan didn’t find any signs of cancer, it detected something else. An aneurysm: a weak spot in the body’s main artery that causes it to balloon.

I was baffled. I was in my mid-fifties and healthy. I had no family history of cardiovascular issues. I was a longtime runner. I ate my veggies and hadn’t had a drink in 27 years. My resting heart rate was borderline smug.

Further tests revealed the diameter of my aorta to be twice the normal size. Putting me at risk of an aortic dissection or rupture, both life-threatening emergencies that demand immediate treatment.

Damn. How long had I been walking—and running—around with this fault line trembling in my chest?

While waiting for an appointment with a cardiologist, I was seized with anxiety. I stopped exercising. I practiced randomly unlocking the emergency feature on my phone and quickly making a mental note of my location.

An echocardiogram later revealed that the bulge had also pulled apart the leaflets of my aortic valve, preventing them from sealing tightly. With every heartbeat, some of the blood my heart pumped out leaked backward, forcing it to work harder to circulate the same blood twice.

“Given that you’re only in your fifties and live an active lifestyle,” the cardiologist said, “I’d suggest you consult with a cardiac surgeon.”

The last sentence I thought I’d ever hear. Until I was met with, “Let’s schedule you for open-heart surgery.”

Looking back, I wondered if there had been signs. I had tried to run at least one marathon or ultra a year, along with some shorter distances. In recent years, no matter how hard I trained, I could never improve my times, my marathons creeping up from low four hours to a whisper below five. I increasingly had to run/walk the final miles. I tried a vegan diet to improve my energy and switched to forefoot running for more spring in my stride. Nothing budged. Maybe I was just getting older.

Gradually, and then seemingly all at once, running became a grind. I started cutting workouts short. The hills felt steeper. The part I looked forward to most was stopping. The joy I had always found in movement was supplanted by fatigue and frustration and more frequent visits to my physical therapist. After plodding across the finish line at the 2025 Falmouth Road Race, I hit the pause button and wondered if I’d ever press play again.

Running has been part of my identity for most of my adult life. After years of flailing, it showed me I was capable. It soothed the anxieties of sobriety and helped me believe I was more than the drunken jerk many people knew when I was in my teens and twenties. It was a sandbox for role-playing difficult conversations, reckoning with my trespasses, and cultivating humility. It was where the idea for my first book took shape and stories took root. It was a way to find people like me, if only through those knowing waves as we passed. Running was more than a healthy habit. It was a partner, my better half.

After all these years, had I fallen out of love? And if I had, who would I be without it?

Open-heart surgery involves slicing through the chest, sawing the sternum in two, parting the halves with a retractor, and stopping the heart. The task of keeping you alive is outsourced to a machine. Even though doctors have been successfully performing this procedure for decades, when it’s you going up on that table, it feels like science fiction.

As the date of my surgery crept closer, fear and anxiety filled me like a helium balloon. The idea of intubation kept me up at night. What if I wake gagging and rip the tube out?

I calmed myself the way I would before a big race: meditation, yoga, and Peggy Huddleston’s pre-surgery relaxation techniques. I studied “the course” and sought out people who’d been through it, looking for any kind of mental edge. And though I was not a religious person, I asked friends and family for prayers, having read that they’d been shown to influence outcomes.

Early one morning in February, I was wheeled into an operating bay at Massachusetts General Hospital, knocked unconscious and chemically paralyzed. Over the next five hours, my surgeon removed my diseased aortic root and ascending aorta, replaced them with a synthetic graft and carbon valve, and hooked my coronary arteries back up to the new plumbing.

When they took me off bypass, my heart forgot how to beat. Instead of pumping, it quivered, seized by electrical chaos. Ventricular fibrillation. The doctors had to shock my heart back into rhythm. Four times. Inside the cardiac OR, the team was ready. Anywhere else, it would have been goodnight, Irene.

I knew none of this when I groggily opened my eyes in the ICU that evening. I felt trampled. I could see the breathing tube that had haunted me for weeks protruding from my mouth, my hands bound to the bedrail to keep me from reaching for it, but I felt no urge, couldn’t feel it. The second time I woke up—the first just brief enough to realize where I was—a voice said, “Squeeze my hand.” My eyelids too heavy to lift, I managed, then drifted back into blackness. When I stirred again, the tube was gone. Relief. But drainage lines snaked from my chest into canisters, while wires and catheters tethered me to a forest of blinking monitors.

Later, in the step-down cardiac ward, I needed a walker to cover even the shortest distance, the drainage boxes hanging on the sides like hard saddlebags. I was carrying 15 extra pounds of fluid, my fingers fat as cocktail wieners. I shuffled down the hall in grippy socks, a tech beside me and a chair trailing behind should I need to sit.

I spent a week at Mass General, three months of recovery ahead of me. In the early weeks, the focus was on walking. Three minutes at a time. Twice a day. Getting to the end of the block took effort. My wife (stone-cold angel!) set up chairs on the landing so I could stop and catch my breath going upstairs in our house outside of Boston. Instead of crushing miles, I was crushing naps.

At six weeks, I met with my surgeon for a follow-up. She was pleased with my progress and lifted some restrictions and cleared me for cardiac rehab. She showed me a picture of my valve leaflets riddled with holes. Told me the aneurysm had likely been there for a decade, the aortic wall “paper thin.” I felt dizzy as if peering over the edge of a tall building. You hear about runners collapsing at the end of marathons, about shovelers going down after a snowstorm. Had it only been a matter of time?

As she described the repair—a Bentall procedure, one of the more complex operations in cardiac surgery—a seductive thought wormed its way into my brain. Sure, aging may have started to slow me down, but a leaky, punctured valve must have been robbing my body of strength and energy, too. Now that a set of brand-new carbon leaflets was opening and closing tightly, blood safely moving in the right direction, could I get my running back on track? Maybe emerge stronger and faster, start breaking PRs again. Could I fall back in love?

I stared at my surgeon, the woman who had held my heart in her hands. Had she seen that old spark still flickering in there?

Cardiac rehab is part safety net, part exercise boot camp. A mini gym with EKG leads and blood-pressure cuffs. When I walked in, an elderly woman in jeans pedaled a recumbent bike while a silver-haired man in a rugby shirt and mask worked an arm cycle. Nearby, an old man plucked one of the resistance ropes that hung from hooks like a swarm of eels. Not everyone had undergone surgery. Some were recovering from heart attacks or stent procedures, others from dangerous arrhythmias or heart failure. I didn’t see anyone else my age.

A physical therapist named Andi asked about my surgery and fitness history, then my goals.

“The seven-mile Falmouth Road Race in four months,” I said. Returning a year later, with a sternum fused by wire, felt like a symbolic milestone. For good measure, I added, “and a marathon next spring.”

I leaned back, waiting for her eyes to light up with amazement. I bet she didn’t hear that very often. She kept scribbling. Probably too stunned, I figured.

She handed me a laminated workout card. “No treadmill?” I frowned. “Soon. Let’s see how you do with these exercises.”

I climbed onto a stationary bike and quietly turned the resistance a few notches above the prescribed setting. I watched my heart rate climb on the monitor above the nurse’s station: 100, 110, 120. Sweat prickled my forehead. That old feeling. For almost two months, my body had belonged to surgeons, nurses, and restrictions. Now, little by little, it would be returned to its rightful owner.

Andi kept her promise. A few weeks later, she prescribed one minute of running. Sixty seconds at a 14-minute pace, followed by two minutes of walking. Five intervals. Three-quarters of a mile. The longest I’d run in eight months. It felt every bit as satisfying as finishing a marathon.

As I built from one-minute intervals to two, then three, I stopped thinking so much about future PRs and training plans. I was running again. The minutes stretched. The walks grew shorter. The weeks passed. By the third month, I was running two miles continuously and sweating so much that the EKG leads kept popping off my chest. Andi would laugh and hand me a fresh set.

When I arrived, I’d seen those sticky leads as signs that I was still a patient. Now they wouldn’t stay on, blanking out my little section on the wall monitor.

On August 16, 2026, I stood among the heaving throngs on Water Street in Woods Hole, the staging area for the Falmouth Road Race on Cape Cod. I stroked my chest. Still tender six months later. Amid shouts and laughter, selfies and the sharp medicinal smell of Bengay mixed with sunscreen, my mind hummed with questions: Was I still the runner I used to be? Did we have a future together? Had my slump been caused by my heart—or “my heart?”

Every few minutes, the crowd surged forward, then stopped, then surged again—an electrical current passing through thousands of bodies as waves of runners were slowly released onto the course.

At last we crossed the starting line. As I set off, an old familiar voice rose to taunt me: This doesn’t count as your big comeback if you take walk breaks, and Dave McGillivray ran the entire Boston Marathon six months after heart surgery.

But then the race gave me something else to listen to. The pounding of rubber soles like golf applause. Spectators shaking cowbells and waving signs. The theme song from “Rocky” pouring from unseen speakers at Nobska Light. The cheers rose around us, and somewhere beyond them the waters of Vineyard Sound flashed in the sun, the island a squiggle on the horizon. Then an emptiness settled over the salty air.

I found myself thinking about who I had become. Or maybe who I’d spent my adult life trying to become. The abstinent runner. The marathoner chasing his father’s PR. The ultrarunner. The trail runner, leaping logs and picking my way across rocks with my trusty dog trotting beside me. Every few years, another version of myself to reel in.

Maybe, for the first time, I needed to stop fishing for some future version of myself. Maybe that was the gift of starting over: the chance to be a beginner again. Who I was 20 years ago. The overweight lug, freshly sober, shuffling down a dirt road in Vermont in the predawn blackness, listening to cicadas and coyotes, watching for flattened frogs and gravel stones the size of baby shoes. The accretion of feeling, competence, and the desire to be a better person. I didn’t know what a PR was. Or a starting corral. My finish line was the sunrise over the Green Mountains. Something I could never reach, only watch in awe. Back when distant light was all I needed.

Every few miles of the race, I walked for a minute. No earbuds. A friend ran beside me, an easy presence, and we chatted, and sometimes we didn’t. The race was everything I’d hoped it would be, which is to say: nothing. No expectations. No aspirations. Pace didn’t matter. I only checked my watch to make sure my heart rate didn’t climb above 180. Falmouth reminded me of a few things: that we are remarkably resilient, that the ocean never fails to awe, and, according to one spectator’s sign, that you should never “trust a fart after mile 6.”

When I crossed the finish line, I raised my arms perfunctorily and smiled for the photographers, lifting my shirt to flash my scar like I was at Mardi Gras. But on the drive home, the emptiness lingered. No epiphany. No transformation. No cinematic moment of rebirth.

I had run seven miles. And somehow, that was all.

That old blah feeling persisted. It took me longer to get out the door, my pace stuck in the basement. So I put a half marathon on the books.

A rare fall nor’easter blew into town one Friday and was still raging on Sunday: rain and wind blowing sideways, tree branches nearly horizontal, deck furniture scattered. I was behind in my training and needed to get a long run in that weekend. I hemmed and hawed for a couple of hours, hoping it would let up. It didn’t.

Finally, I got dressed. My Garmin had died the week before, so I set off blind. No pace, distance, or heart-rate information. By the time I reached the bike path along the Charles, my clothes were plastered to my skin. Broken branches and leaves littered the pavement. It looked like the aftermath of a house party. Rain hammered the river. With a playlist in my ears, I felt as if I were running through an adventure movie.

Cars sent waves of water rolling over the guardrails. Enormous puddles swamped the path. At first I tried to avoid them. Then I realized there was no point, and it became fun. I splashed through them like a kid.

I was the only one out there. Despite the wild weather, everything felt quiet, abandoned. And somehow that spurred me on. A small tree had fallen across a wooden footbridge. I had to wrestle it out of the way. Storylines bubbled up. I was racing to the next town after a catastrophic event, seeking help; lives depended on me. I had to keep going.

Finally, I saw another runner, both of us looking like we’d been fished out of a lake. We waved—not perfunctorily, but with a knowing look. Was he running for help, too?

The slap of my feet on wet asphalt took over the soundtrack, along with the gusts of my own breathing and the faint ticking of my mechanical valve in my throat. I had no idea how far I’d gone or how much farther I had to go.

For once, I didn’t need to know. I felt inside and outside everything at the same time, the rain somehow lighting the way.

Caleb Daniloff is a Boston-area writer and author of Running Ransom Road: Confronting The Past One Marathon at a Time and co-author of November Project: The Book: Inside the Free Grassroots Fitness Movement That’s Taking Over The World.

It includes Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, Nvidia, Alphabet (Google), Meta, Berkshire Hathaway, and approximately 493 other companies that collectively represent about 80% of the total U.S. stock market value.

The index is maintained by S&P Dow Jones Indices, which periodically adds and removes companies based on criteria including market cap (must exceed ~$18 billion), profitability, liquidity, and domicile. When a company is added to the S&P 500, every index fund tracking it automatically buys shares — and vice versa when companies are removed.

An S&P 500 index fund is a mutual fund or exchange-traded fund (ETF) that holds all 500 stocks in the same proportions as the index. Instead of picking individual stocks, you buy one fund and instantly own a piece of every major U.S. company. The fund mechanically replicates the index — no stock picking, no market timing, no overpaid fund managers.

The data is overwhelming. Over any 15-year period, approximately 92% of actively managed large-cap funds underperform the S&P 500 after fees, according to the SPIVA scorecard. Over 20 years, that number exceeds 95%. The reasons are simple: active fund managers charge 0.50% to 1.50% in annual fees, they generate taxable trading activity, and they cannot consistently pick winners.

Warren Buffett bet $1 million that an S&P 500 index fund would beat a selection of hedge funds over 10 years. He won decisively — the index fund returned 125.8% vs 36.0% for the hedge fund basket. As Buffett has said: "By periodically investing in an index fund, the know-nothing investor can actually outperform most investment professionals."

The top S&P 500 index funds deliver nearly identical performance because they all track the same index. The differences come down to expense ratio, minimum investment, fund structure (ETF vs mutual fund), and tax efficiency. Here is a detailed comparison of the five most popular options.

The most popular S&P 500 ETF and the default recommendation for most FI seekers. At 0.03% expense ratio, a $500,000 investment costs just $150 per year in fees. VOO is tax-efficient due to the ETF structure and Vanguard's patented heartbeat trade process, which minimizes capital gains distributions. Fractional shares are available at most brokerages.

The lowest-cost S&P 500 fund available at 0.015% — half the cost of VOO. No minimum investment requirement makes it ideal for beginners. As a mutual fund, you can set up automatic investments in exact dollar amounts (e.g., $500/month). FXAIX is an excellent choice if your brokerage is Fidelity.

BlackRock's S&P 500 ETF with a 0.03% expense ratio, matching VOO. Functionally identical performance. Slightly different creation/redemption mechanics than VOO but the practical difference for individual investors is negligible. A strong alternative if you prefer iShares or trade through a brokerage that offers commission-free iShares ETFs.

The oldest and most heavily traded S&P 500 ETF, launched in 1993. SPY is the most liquid ETF in the world, making it the preferred choice for active traders. However, its 0.0945% expense ratio is over three times higher than VOO or IVV. For long-term FI investors, VOO or IVV are better choices. SPY's structure as a unit investment trust also makes it slightly less tax-efficient than VOO.

Schwab's mutual fund offering at 0.02% expense ratio with no minimum investment. Like FXAIX, the mutual fund structure allows automatic dollar-amount investing. An excellent choice for Schwab customers building automated investment plans.

Investing in an S&P 500 fund takes less than 15 minutes:

For retirement accounts (401k, IRA), look for the S&P 500 index fund option within your plan. It may have a different name (e.g., "Large Cap Index Fund" or "Institutional S&P 500") but will track the same index.

The total stock market index (tracked by VTI/VTSAX/FSKAX) holds approximately 3,600 stocks compared to the S&P 500's 500. The additional 3,100 stocks are mid-cap and small-cap companies. Here is how they compare:

Historically, the performance difference between the two is minimal — typically within 0.1-0.3% per year in either direction. The S&P 500 has outperformed in periods when large-cap growth stocks dominate. The total market has outperformed when small and mid-cap stocks lead. Over 20+ year periods, the returns converge closely.

The FI community's honest answer: it does not matter much which you choose. Investing $25,500 per year in VOO or VTI will produce nearly identical outcomes over 20 years. Consistency and contribution amount matter far more than the choice between S&P 500 and total market.

S&P 500 index funds typically yield 1.2% to 1.6% in annual dividends. In a tax-advantaged account (401k, IRA, Roth), dividends compound tax-free. In a taxable account, qualified dividends from S&P 500 funds are taxed at the favorable long-term capital gains rate (0%, 15%, or 20% depending on income).

ETFs (VOO, IVV) are generally more tax-efficient than mutual funds (FXAIX, SWPPX) in taxable accounts because ETFs rarely distribute capital gains. Vanguard's mutual funds are an exception — their patented ETF share class structure gives Vanguard mutual funds ETF-like tax efficiency. For taxable brokerage accounts, VOO or VFIAX (Vanguard's mutual fund version) are the most tax-efficient choices.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

The most common mistake with S&P 500 index funds is waiting for the "right time" to invest. Research from Vanguard shows that investing a lump sum immediately outperforms dollar-cost averaging about two-thirds of the time, because markets go up more often than they go down. Missing just the 10 best trading days over a 20-year period can cut your returns nearly in half. If you have money to invest, the data overwhelmingly says to invest it now — not next week, not after the next pullback, not when it "feels right."

Open an account at Vanguard (for VOO/VFIAX), Fidelity (for FXAIX), or Schwab (for SWPPX). All three offer commission-free trading on their own index funds, excellent customer service, and robust retirement account options. You can also buy any of these funds at most brokerages.

ETFs (VOO, IVV) trade like stocks at real-time prices and are more tax-efficient in taxable accounts. Mutual funds (FXAIX, SWPPX) allow automatic dollar-amount investing and are better for set-it-and-forget-it contribution schedules. For retirement accounts, either works equally well.

Transfer cash to your brokerage account and buy your chosen fund. Start with whatever you have — there is no minimum too small. FXAIX and SWPPX have $0 minimums, and VOO can be purchased in fractional shares at most brokerages for as little as $1.

Automate monthly or per-paycheck contributions. This removes emotion from the process and ensures consistent dollar-cost averaging. Most brokerages let you schedule recurring purchases of mutual funds. For ETFs, some brokerages offer automatic ETF purchases as well.

If you hold other asset classes (bonds, international), rebalance once per year to maintain your target allocation. Otherwise, do nothing — do not check daily prices, do not sell during downturns, and do not chase performance. The S&P 500 has recovered from every crash in history. Time in the market beats timing the market.

Fidelity 500 Index Fund (FXAIX) has the lowest expense ratio at 0.015%. Schwab S&P 500 Index Fund (SWPPX) is next at 0.02%. VOO and IVV tie at 0.03%. All four are excellent — the fee difference between FXAIX (0.015%) and VOO (0.03%) on a $500,000 portfolio is just $75 per year. Choose the fund offered by your preferred brokerage.

VOO is better for long-term investors. It charges 0.03% vs SPY's 0.0945%, saving you about $325 per year on a $500,000 portfolio. VOO is also more tax-efficient due to its ETF share class structure. SPY's advantage is liquidity for active trading, which long-term index investors do not need. For buy-and-hold FI investing, VOO is the clear winner.

Either is an excellent choice. The S&P 500 covers approximately 80% of the U.S. stock market by value. A total market fund adds mid-cap and small-cap stocks for fuller diversification. Over long periods, performance is nearly identical — typically within 0.1-0.3% per year. The FI community consensus is that the best fund is the one you will consistently invest in without overthinking the decision.

As little as $1. FXAIX and SWPPX have zero minimum investments. VOO and IVV can be purchased as fractional shares at most brokerages. There is no minimum too small — starting with $50 or $100 per month and increasing contributions as your income grows is exactly how most people on the FI path begin.

The S&P 500 has returned approximately 10.3% per year on average since 1957 (including dividends). Adjusted for inflation, the real return is approximately 7.0% per year. These are long-term averages — individual years range from -38% (2008) to +38% (1995). The key is staying invested through the down years to capture the recovery gains that follow.

S&P 500 index funds carry market risk — they can lose significant value in the short term (the index dropped 34% in early 2020 and 38% in 2008). However, the S&P 500 has recovered from every decline in its history and has never lost money over any 20-year period. For investors with a 10+ year time horizon, the risk of not investing (missing out on 10% average annual returns) is far greater than the risk of temporary market declines.

S&P 500 index funds are the single most important building block for long-term wealth. With expense ratios as low as 0.015%, you keep virtually all of your returns while owning a piece of the 500 largest U.S. companies. VOO, FXAIX, IVV, and SWPPX all deliver near-identical performance — choose the fund offered by your preferred brokerage and automate your contributions. The FI community has proven through thousands of real-world examples that consistent investing in a low-cost S&P 500 index fund, held for decades without panic selling, is the most reliable path to building wealth and reaching financial independence.

#8688. Start the Day Strong With This 30-Minute Workout You Can Do Right at Home

Burn every muscle of the body while revving the heart rate.

An at-home workout that requires zero equipment might sound easy—but this one will change your mind! The fun, challenging exercises (all bodyweight!) target every major muscle of the body, which means you make the most of just 30 minutes of work. Squeeze it in before you head out for the day or whenever you need a movement break today; it’s easy to fit in at any time.

Dane Miklaus, C.S.C.S., founder of WORK Training Studio in Idaho, took on the puzzle of creating this tough, no-equipment workout and pieced together a creative routine to get your muscles firing on all fronts. Consider it your go-to during a busy holiday schedule.

“I chose to focus on areas where traditional endurance athletes may have weaknesses due to underutilization,” Miklaus tells Runner’s World. Because running and most of our daily movements occur in the sagittal plane of motion—that’s forward and backward—we tend to neglect muscles used in lateral (or side-to-side) and rotational movements, causing weakness in these areas. While that not only leads to suboptimal performance, it can also increase your risk of injury, he explains.

“By implementing a lower-body routine that incorporates lateral and rotational movements, as well as upper-body and core training, runners can increase their overall athletic standards and the functional capacity of their bodies,” Miklaus says.

In addition to making you move in different planes of motion, this workout also alternates lower-body and upper-body or core exercises. That way, one muscle group gets rest as the other works, Miklaus explains, without you having to take much actual rest time.

The lower-body moves also get more difficult as you work through the seven-exercise circuit, while the upper-body ones become less intense. “This is intended to provide a balanced challenge and allow each athlete space to scale the difficulty [of the workout] to their own fitness level,” Miklaus explains.

How to do the workout: Do each exercise in order for 45 seconds. Rest for 15 seconds while also transitioning into the next move. Repeat for four total sets.

You don’t need any equipment for this workout, but an exercise mat is optional. Miklaus demonstrates each exercise in the video above so you can learn proper form.

Why it works: Target the muscles that support the hips—including the gluteus medius and minimus (the smaller backside muscles) and the piriformis (deep butt muscle)—as well as the hamstrings, adductors (inner thighs), and gluteus maximus (biggest muscle of the butt). “A more stable hip is a stronger hip, and because runners rely on their hips for every stride, exercises like these are a must,” Miklaus says.

Why it works: While you’ll hit your chest and shoulders, push-ups are also great for strengthening the deep core muscles and shoulder stabilizers, Miklaus says. The shoulder tap also adds an anti-rotation element to turn up the core-stability challenge.

Why it works: “When all you have for equipment is in your own bodyweight, adding a speed or power component is a great way to increase muscular recruitment,” Miklaus says. “So, by dropping into the squat and absorbing that force, then rebounding back out of it quickly, we turn on more of our leg muscles than if we performed a basic bodyweight squat.” The twist at the top means more fire in the rotational hip and core muscles, too.

Why it works: While runners get some biceps activation on the run during the arm swing, they often neglect their triceps, Miklaus says. This move changes that, plus it still taps into core strength.

Why it works: Build hip strength and stability with this exercise that creates a “triple extension” a.k.a. when the hip, knee, and ankle joints all get in on the action.

Plus, “just like with the drop squat, this single-leg hop variation will recruit almost every fiber in an athlete’s glutes, quads, and calves, to make them more forceful and dynamic,” Miklaus says. “What runner couldn’t stand to be a bit more explosive?”

Why it works: “When performing bodyweight exercises, it’s very difficult to stimulate the back muscles,” Miklaus says. But this move activates the latissimus dorsi (major muscle of the back), teres major, and posterior deltoid (both on the back of the shoulder). “This is important for helping to provide postural balance for athletes who only incorporate pushing movements into their upper-body routines,” he adds. Finally, the plank hold with knee drive means your abs and obliques get worked, too.

Why it works: The skater exercise forces you to slow down momentum, stabilize, and then explode again, Miklaus explains. “When moving laterally, and into a hinged position, we are able to recruit more of the deep hip muscles than is possible when only moving in the sagittal plane,” he says. In addition to strengthening muscles at the hip, it also improves ankle stability.

Mallory Creveling is an ACE-certified personal trainer and RRCA-certified run coach, who also holds certifications in kettlebell training, sports performance, and more. She has more than 15 years of experience covering fitness, health, and nutrition for a wide range of publications, and nearly 10 years of experience as a trainer and fitness instructor. Mallory stays on top of her continuing education in fitness, as well as the latest science in wellness. She has worked with some of the best experts in their medical fields, and regularly interviews researchers, trainers, athletes, and more to find the best advice for readers looking to improve their performance and well-being. As a freelance writer, Mallory's work appeared in Women's Health, Self, Men's Journal, Reader's Digest, and more. She has also held staff editorial positions at Family Circle and Shape magazines, as well as DailyBurn.com. A former New Yorker/Brooklynite, she's now based in Easton, Pennsylvania.
